# Aligning Autoresearch: Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans

Tianjian Li    Chuanyang Jin    Seungone Kim    Tong Chen    John
Hoffman Affiliation: FAIR at Meta     
Yoram Bachrach Affiliation: FAIR at Meta    Pedro Rodriguez
Affiliation: FAIR at Meta    Ping Yu Affiliation: FAIR at Meta    Eryk
Helenowski Affiliation: FAIR at Meta    Swarnadeep Saha
Affiliation: FAIR at Meta     
Jack Lanchantin    Weizhe Yuan    Ilia Kulikov    Jason Weston
Affiliation: Johns Hopkins University Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon
University Affiliation: University of Washington

###### Abstract

Autoresearch agents can now attempt long-horizon AI research end-to-end,
i.e., self-improvement. However, best results are still obtained by
research agents interacting with human researchers, and improving AI’s
ability to perform this co-research will only reinforce this effect—a
process termed co-improvement ([Weston and Foerster,
2025](#bib.bib137)). Further, aligning with humans is likely a safer
path for research agents, especially given recent agent reward hacking
phenomena ([OpenAI, 2026b](#bib.bib98)). In this work we address these
issues in four ways: (i) we empirically study the role of humans in
directing autoresearch agents, focusing on the domain of benchmark
creation, and find humans still play a pivotal role particularly in the
ideation phase; (ii) we develop a benchmark, HackBench, that shows
current autoresearch agents are not aligned and are unable to achieve
hack localization sufficiently; (iii) we present a method to train
agents for improved human interaction by using human simulators as a
proxy during reinforcement learning (RL); and finally (iv) we develop a
method to improve model text generation, and hence agent communication,
by RL with rubrics aligned with human experts. Together, our training
and evaluation recipes provide a path toward more capable and aligned
(co-)research agents.

^(†)^(†)date: October 28, 2026

## 1 The role of humans in directing research agents for benchmark creation

### 1.1 Overview

As autoresearch agents and recursive self-improvement (RSI) draw
increasing attention, determining how models should direct their own
improvement is becoming more important ([Yin et al., 2025](#bib.bib154);
[Anthropic, 2026](#bib.bib5); [Weng, 2026](#bib.bib136)). While strong
evidence shows that some verifiable tasks can be successfully automated
(e.g., tasks that require hill-climbing a pre-defined metric ([Wijk
et al., 2025](#bib.bib139); [Chan et al., 2025](#bib.bib15); [Karpathy,
2026](#bib.bib57))), the scope and necessity of human contribution in
open-ended tasks remain open questions. We focus on one such area,
benchmark creation. Specifically, curating problems that are both
difficult and meaningful to solve is a crucial task in AI model
development ([Reuel et al., 2024](#bib.bib114); [Bean et al.,
2026](#bib.bib12); [Singh et al., 2026](#bib.bib120)). From an
evaluation perspective, it allows researchers to analyze the
capabilities that models currently lack; from a development perspective,
it supplies new targets to hill-climb on ([Liang et al.,
2022](#bib.bib71); [Chang et al., 2024](#bib.bib16)).

To date, benchmark creation is driven mainly by human AI scientists, and
the process is fairly laborious. One first decides what the benchmark is
meant to measure or assess (i.e., the construct), then identifies the
grounding material used to instantiate it (e.g., GitHub PRs for
SWE-Bench ([Jimenez et al., 2024](#bib.bib51))), then designs a pipeline
through which problems are produced and model predictions are evaluated,
and finally runs the evaluation, iterating over these steps. The process
further branches into granular decisions across an effectively unbounded
space of possibilities: errors in the pipeline code must be fixed,
strategies for increasing difficulty must be devised when problems prove
insufficiently hard, and humans must be brought into the loop wherever
verification is needed. In short, there is no unified recipe for
building a high-quality benchmark, and the construction process varies
with the type of benchmark and with the researcher who carries it out.

It is precisely this open-endedness that makes benchmark creation a
demanding test for an autoresearch agent. In particular, we focus on
autoresearch agents that create benchmarks for autoresearch agents:
high-quality autoresearch agent benchmarks remain sparse relative to
question-answering or competition mathematics benchmarks, so
constructing a good one is a meaningful goal in its own right. Moreover,
because autoresearch agent baselines must be run over long horizons,
building such problems together with their surrounding environments
renders benchmark creation considerably harder, and correspondingly more
interesting.

To this end, we introduce AutoBenchmark, a framework in which an
autoresearch agent builds a benchmark from a task specification and
revises it across iterations using two feedback signals: (1) the
trajectories and scores of a set of solvers that attempt the benchmark,
and (2) the critique of an LLM verifier that checks the quality of the
benchmark. Additionally, as a third axis, we investigate if human AI
scientists can contribute to this process by directing what to build at
the start of the loop and advising on revisions between iterations.

Our experiments show that current autoresearch agents can run this loop
end to end, but that the benchmarks they produce unaided (i.e., without
human feedback) are close to saturated, allowing the solvers to achieve
scores above 80. We also find that human feedback helps substantially,
and the gain grows with how specific that feedback is. Specifically,
providing detailed direction on what type of benchmark to build and how
to build it halves the score of the solvers, while a brief statement of
what to build helps only marginally. This indicates that human
involvement is still required in benchmark creation. Looking ahead, we
envision AutoBenchmark as a way to measure progress on the capability of
AI agents to autonomously create or co-create high-quality benchmarks.

![Refer to caption](2610.38882v1/autobenchmarking.png)

Figure 1: AutoBenchmark: evaluating the ability of autoresearch agents
to create benchmarks. AutoBenchmark instructs an autoresearch agent to
create a benchmark; we specifically target benchmarks that evaluate
autoresearch agents themselves (i.e., benchmarking autoresearch). Within
the benchmark creation loop, the autoresearch agent iteratively revises
the benchmark via two main sources of feedback: one from the benchmark
solvers (including the same model used as the benchmark creator) and the
other from external verifiers of the benchmark (AI or human). We thus
also study if having humans provide additional feedback on what
benchmark to make and how to make it helps or not.

### 1.2 AutoBenchmark

[Figure 1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1.1 Overview ‣ 1 The role of humans in directing research agents for benchmark creation ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")shows
the overall design of AutoBenchmark, in which a research agent is asked
to carry out the benchmark creation process end-to-end. The research
agent produces a benchmark in a Harbor-compatible evaluation
package ([Harbor Framework Team, 2026](#bib.bib40)): a container
environment, task instructions, the evidence supplied to the solver,
reference solution, and machine-checkable grading criteria. The
AutoBenchmark pipeline consists of the following stages (further details
are in
[Appendix A](#A1 "Appendix A AutoBenchmark implementation details ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")):

Stage 1: Benchmark Proposal. The goal in this stage is to create
difficult yet high-quality tasks. The research agent receives a task
spec (a file that contains a general set of rules and, when a human
provides feedback at the proposal stage, that direction as well; in the
fully autonomous setting the file carries the rules alone) and,
optionally, grounding material, and decides what capability the
benchmark should measure before deciding how to measure it. It writes
down the construct, develops several materially different ways to
operationalize it, searches for and stores the primary sources it relies
on, and then instantiates the selected design as a set of runnable
tasks. Because the package has to execute, the agent also owns the
decisions a human benchmark designer normally owns: what the solver
sees, what evidence it is given, what an ideal answer contains, how
partial credit is assigned, and a reference solution that shows the task
can be solved at all.

Stage 2: Benchmark Solving. Each task is attempted by one or more solver
agents inside the environment the research agent specified. Every
attempt produces a trajectory and a final answer, and an answer judge
grades that answer against the criteria the research agent wrote. These
scores give the loop its difficulty signal, since a benchmark that the
solvers already saturate tells us little about the frontier.

Stage 3: Benchmark Review. A low solver score on its own is weak
evidence, because a broken task, an unsatisfiable requirement, a
mis-specified grader, and fabricated grounding all produce the same
number. An agent that optimizes solver failure alone also has an easy
degenerate strategy available to it, which is to make the tasks
impossible. We therefore review the benchmark itself, using an LLM judge
that is applied to the research agent rather than to the solvers, along
five criteria: construct validity, correctness, feasibility, usefulness,
and an overall verdict. The resulting verdicts decide whether an
iteration is eligible to be built on.

Below, in addition to the overall pipeline specified above, we list the
components within each stage:

Component 1: Autodata Loop. Inspired by Autodata ([Kulikov et al.,
2026](#bib.bib65)), in AutoBenchmark, the research agent alternates
creation and analysis until the iteration budget is exhausted. Each
iteration is seeded from the best checkpoint so far, so a revision that
(1) the judges reject, or (2) makes the solver achieve a higher score
compared to previous iterations, does not become the checkpoint of the
next revision. The parent of an iteration is therefore the
lowest-scoring accepted iteration so far, which is not necessarily the
immediately preceding one. Feedback is exposed as file-system memory:
frozen snapshots, trajectories, answers, rubric judgments, and verdicts
are written to disk and the prompt names the paths, so the accumulated
history grows over iterations.

Component 2: Detecting reward hacking with external solvers. Optimizing
against a fixed set of solvers risks producing a benchmark that is
adversarially hard for particular models. To detect if such reward
hacking behavior occurs from the benchmark proposer, we evaluate
additional solvers that take no part in the loop and whose results are
never written into the research agent’s feedback. Cheaper external
solvers are run after every iteration, giving a difficulty trace that is
independent of the solvers being optimized against, while more expensive
ones run on the selected best checkpoint.

Component 3: Human involvement. Benchmark creation involves two
decisions, _what_ to measure and _how_ to measure it, and a human can
supply either at different levels of detail. Within the AutoBenchmark
pipeline, we vary both, together with whether human feedback is
available only before the run or also during it, giving four settings:

- (i)
  No feedback. The run is fully autonomous. The agent receives no human
  direction and no grounding, only the general rules of the task spec,
  and chooses the scientific domain, the construct, and the
  operationalization itself.
- (ii)
  Coarse-grained human feedback (proposal stage). A human states the
  intent in a single sentence (e.g., what the benchmark should target).
  This fixes _what_ to measure while leaving the entire
  operationalization to the agent.
- (iii)
  Fine-grained human feedback (proposal stage). A human writes a
  detailed task specification and additionally curates the list of
  grounding material the agent may use. This fixes both _what_ to
  measure and much of _how_, and corresponds to the level of direction a
  human benchmark designer would decide before work starts.
- (iv)
  Fine-grained human feedback (proposal & execution stage). In addition
  to (iii), a human inspects the outcome of a given iteration and writes
  what the agent should do next, so that direction is also available
  _during_ the loop.

### 1.3 Experimental Setup

Choice of models. We use Muse Spark 1.1 as the research agent that
proposes the benchmark. We use Muse Spark 1.1 itself together with
Muse-Glimmer-30B as the solvers inside the loop, giving a setting in
which the proposer attempts to create problems that a considerably
weaker model and the proposer itself cannot solve, yet that remain
meaningful. Unlike Autodata ([Kulikov et al., 2026](#bib.bib65)), we
therefore do not assume the existence of a strong solver that certifies
correctness; creating problems that the proposer itself cannot solve
aligns more closely with the purpose of benchmark curation, since the
frontier models can always be integrated as part of the AutoBenchmark
pipeline. Muse Spark 1.1 also serves as the answer judge and as the five
benchmark-quality judges. As external solvers, we use
NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B after every iteration and
Claude-Opus-5 on the selected best checkpoint; neither is integrated in
the loop.

Grounding material & Built benchmarks. In the settings where grounding
material is supplied ((iii) and (iv)), the harness gives the research
agent a corpus of primary sources. Specifically, the harness hashes
every source and snapshots it read-only before the session starts, and
the agent may additionally retrieve public web content during the
grounding stage. We experiment with three automatically generated
autoresearch benchmarks developed by our method:

1.  (1)
    Graveyard Bench (ideation): Can AI assistants avoid proposing
    dead-end ideas? The benchmark is grounded in documented negative
    results, namely research directions that the scientific record shows
    were pursued and abandoned. We draw on the medical-reversals
    supplement of [Herrera-Perez et al. (2019)](#bib.bib41), which
    catalogs clinical practices later overturned by subsequent
    randomized trials; registry records from ClinicalTrials.gov ([U.S.
    National Library of Medicine, 2026](#bib.bib128)) together with
    their aggregated form in AACT ([Clinical Trials Transformation
    Initiative, 2026](#bib.bib20)), which document trials whose reported
    outcomes fail to support the hypothesis under test; and the
    Reproducibility Project: Psychology ([Open Science Collaboration,
    2015](#bib.bib96)), which records effects that do not survive direct
    replication. An agent is tasked to propose an idea and is scored on
    whether that proposed direction has already been foreclosed.
2.  (2)
    SilentTrain Bench (experimentation): Can AI assistants patch buggy
    code that silently degrades performance? The benchmark is grounded
    in defects that leave a training run executable while lowering the
    metric it reports, so that no error trace is available to localize
    the fault. We source these from the silent-error corpus released
    with TrainCheck ([Jiang et al., 2025](#bib.bib50)), and from the
    commit histories of two kinds of repository. The first are widely
    used training frameworks and libraries: PyTorch ([Paszke et al.,
    2019](#bib.bib105)), TensorFlow ([Abadi et al., 2016](#bib.bib1)),
    HuggingFace Transformers ([Wolf et al., 2020](#bib.bib140)) and
    Accelerate ([Gugger et al., 2022](#bib.bib38)), DeepSpeed ([Rasley
    et al., 2020](#bib.bib113)), PyTorch Lightning ([Falcon and The
    PyTorch Lightning team, 2019](#bib.bib29)),
    torchvision ([TorchVision maintainers and contributors,
    2016](#bib.bib126)) and timm ([Wightman, 2019](#bib.bib138)),
    Detectron2 ([Wu et al., 2019](#bib.bib145)), vLLM ([Kwon et al.,
    2023](#bib.bib67)), LitGPT ([Lightning AI, 2023](#bib.bib74)),
    Mosaic Composer ([The Mosaic ML Team, 2021](#bib.bib125)),
    OpenNMT-py ([Klein et al., 2017](#bib.bib63)), and lmms-eval ([Zhang
    et al., 2024](#bib.bib163)). The second are self-contained research
    codebases, whose narrower scope makes a degradation attributable to
    a single defect: nanoGPT ([Karpathy, 2022](#bib.bib56)) for
    language-model pretraining, ring-flash-attention ([Zhu,
    2024](#bib.bib171)) for long-context attention, opinf ([McQuarrie
    et al., 2023](#bib.bib86)) for operator inference on dynamical
    systems, GrowNet ([Badirli et al., 2020](#bib.bib6)) for
    gradient-boosted neural networks,
    stable-continual-learning ([Mirzadeh et al., 2020](#bib.bib88)) for
    continual learning under varying training regimes,
    Human-Path-Prediction ([Mangalam et al., 2021](#bib.bib83)) for
    pedestrian trajectory forecasting, turboquant-pro ([Zandieh et al.,
    2026](#bib.bib161)) for KV-cache quantization, and mrpro ([MRpro
    Team, 2024](#bib.bib92)) for MR image reconstruction. The GH Archive
    event stream ([Grigorik, 2026](#bib.bib37)) is used to locate the
    relevant commits and issue threads, and training runs are executed
    on Imagenette ([Howard, 2019](#bib.bib43)). An agent is tasked to
    produce a patch that fixes the buggy code and is scored on whether
    its patch restores the performance.
3.  (3)
    Rebuttal Bench (assessment): Can AI assistants determine whether a
    paper rebuttal resolves the weakness raised against a claim? The
    benchmark is grounded in public review threads, which pair a
    reviewer’s stated weakness with the authors’ response and with the
    reviewer’s subsequent reply. We use DISAPERE ([Kennard et al.,
    2022](#bib.bib59)), which annotates review and rebuttal sentences
    with their discourse function and the authors’ stance toward each
    review argument, and PRRCA ([Wu et al., 2022](#bib.bib141)), which
    pairs reviews with rebuttal counter-arguments, alongside raw threads
    from three venues that publish their review correspondence: initial
    and final reviewer scores from ICLR 2024 ([OpenReview,
    2026](#bib.bib99)), the transparent peer-review files of Nature
    Communications ([Nature Communications, 2026](#bib.bib94)), and the
    decision letters and point-by-point responses of eLife ([eLife
    Sciences Publications, 2026](#bib.bib28)). An agent is tasked to
    produce a file that marks if each claim within the rebuttal from the
    author resolves the weakness mentioned by the reviewer, and is
    scored on whether it correctly judges.

Configurations. Every run produces a benchmark with ten instances over
ten iterations, and each solver attempts every task once per iteration,
so an iteration’s difficulty signal is the mean over ten independent
task observations per model. Solvers receive the same execution contract
in every iteration (4 CPUs, 16 GiB of memory, and a 24-hour agent budget
per task, with a separate verifier container for grading the solver’s
submission), so scores stay comparable across iterations. Before any
solver is run, the harness executes the agent’s own reference solution
against the real verifier and admits the submission only when it scores
at least $`0.9`$, returning the iteration for a repair session
otherwise, with at most ten submission attempts per iteration. Each
point in
[Figure 2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1.3 Experimental Setup ‣ 1 The role of humans in directing research agents for benchmark creation ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
(Rebuttal Bench and Graveyard Bench) and
[Figure 3](#S1.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 1.3 Experimental Setup ‣ 1 The role of humans in directing research agents for benchmark creation ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
(SilentTrain Bench) reports a solver’s mean score across the ten tasks
at that iteration. Scores are displayed on a 0–100 scale. Lower scores
indicate a harder (better) benchmark.

### 1.4 Experimental results

Human feedback helps to curate harder and higher-quality benchmarks.
Results in
[Figure 2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1.3 Experimental Setup ‣ 1 The role of humans in directing research agents for benchmark creation ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
show that feedback from humans improves over fully autonomous benchmark
creation, with fine-grained feedback more useful than coarse-grained
feedback. In the fine-grained feedback setting, the research agent is
able to create benchmarks that are both difficult for models, and pass
all validity checks, with generalization of the benchmarks to a held-out
model. Without human feedback, the scores are much higher (hence, the
benchmarks created are already saturated), and more often fail validity
checks as well. We note that as models get more powerful, we expect
these trends to change. AutoBenchmark can hence be used to monitor this
progress. The no-feedback curve is a single autonomous run that chooses
its own benchmark and is reused in both rows of
[Figure 2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1.3 Experimental Setup ‣ 1 The role of humans in directing research agents for benchmark creation ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans").
The fine-grained proposal setting supplies both detailed instructions
and curated grounding material.

When a human intervenes during the proposal stage, the intervention
should be concrete. In
[Figure 2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1.3 Experimental Setup ‣ 1 The role of humans in directing research agents for benchmark creation ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans"),
the selected checkpoint on Rebuttal Bench falls from $`90`$, $`84`$, and
$`80`$ on Muse Spark, Muse Glimmer, and Nemotron with no feedback, to
$`84.4`$, $`83.7`$, and $`81`$ with coarse-grained feedback, and to
$`43.5`$, $`51.2`$, and $`39.1`$ with fine-grained feedback.
Coarse-grained feedback improves (lowers) the score by up to $`13.8`$
points relative to no feedback on Graveyard Bench, but is essentially
flat on Rebuttal Bench, where it moves Muse Glimmer by $`0.3`$ points
($`83.7`$ vs. $`84`$) and leaves Nemotron slightly worse ($`81`$ vs.
$`80`$). Fine-grained feedback, by contrast, improves the score by
$`28`$ to $`46.5`$ points in every one of the six benchmark–solver
pairs. Hence we read this as evidence that the proposal stage is where
human input pays off, in that with the same agent and the same loop,
curating the material it works from yields a substantially harder
benchmark.

Benchmark difficulty transfers to a held-out solver. At the selected
checkpoints in
[Figure 2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1.3 Experimental Setup ‣ 1 The role of humans in directing research agents for benchmark creation ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans"),
Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B scores $`39.1`$ in the fine-grained
proposal feedback setting compared to $`81`$ in the coarse-grained
proposal feedback setting on Rebuttal Bench, and $`52`$ vs. $`75.4`$ on
Graveyard Bench. Hence, we confirm that the resulting benchmark is
genuinely hard not only for Muse Spark and Muse Glimmer but for a
held-out model as well. The ordering also holds for Claude-Opus-5, which
we run only on the selected best checkpoint, as shown in
[Table 1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1.3 Experimental Setup ‣ 1 The role of humans in directing research agents for benchmark creation ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans").

The verifier catches defects that the score cannot see. Across all runs
plotted in
[Figure 2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1.3 Experimental Setup ‣ 1 The role of humans in directing research agents for benchmark creation ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
and
[Figure 3](#S1.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 1.3 Experimental Setup ‣ 1 The role of humans in directing research agents for benchmark creation ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans"),
the benchmark verifier rejects any iteration that violates one of our
five predefined criteria, so that iteration cannot become the parent of
the next.
[Figure 4](#S1.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 1.3 Experimental Setup ‣ 1 The role of humans in directing research agents for benchmark creation ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
shows three examples of quality issues identified by the LLM judges
where solver scores alone would be insufficient: answers leaking into
files the solver can read, a construct too shallow or too memorized to
separate the solvers, and grounding material the creator claims to use
but does not actually retain in the benchmark. A leaked answer key puts
the solvers at ceiling, which looks exactly like a construct that is too
easy, and missing grounding is consistent with any score at all, so
neither defect can be caught by looking at the score. In
[Figure 2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1.3 Experimental Setup ‣ 1 The role of humans in directing research agents for benchmark creation ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans"),
iteration $`5`$ of the fine-grained Rebuttal Bench run scores $`47.4`$,
the lowest of that run so far, and would have seeded iteration $`6`$ had
it not failed the feasibility criterion. The loop continues from
iteration $`3`$ instead, the lowest-scoring accepted iteration at that
point, and reaches $`43.5`$ at iteration $`8`$ with all five criteria
passing.
[Figure 2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1.3 Experimental Setup ‣ 1 The role of humans in directing research agents for benchmark creation ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
shows the reverse for the autonomous run: its first three iterations all
score $`100.0`$ on Muse Spark, and only the verdicts tell them apart,
failing five criteria at iteration $`1`$ and two at iteration $`3`$,
with iteration $`4`$ the first to pass all five. Selecting on score
alone would have kept iterations the verifier rejects.

When the autoresearch loop stalls, human direction helps. As shown in
[Figure 3](#S1.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 1.3 Experimental Setup ‣ 1 The role of humans in directing research agents for benchmark creation ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans"),
through iteration $`5`$ the SilentTrain Bench run appears to stall, with
Muse Spark above $`92`$. We forked the run at iteration $`6`$ and gave
one continuation three human-guided instructions, all of them about
instantiation and none about what to measure: put the solver on a
multi-hour job, build the environment from the complete files in the
grounding material instead of excerpted stand-ins, and grade with
behavioral tests against the original buggy behavior instead of a
deterministic checker. With that guidance the selected checkpoint
reaches $`64.2`$ on Muse Spark compared to $`88.1`$ without it, $`54.2`$
vs. $`85.6`$ on Muse Glimmer, and $`48.8`$ vs. $`83.8`$ on Nemotron,
where the gap is widest. We interpret this as evidence that execution
feedback helps once the agent’s own revisions have stopped working.

### 1.5 Related Work

Automatic benchmark construction.  A line of work asks whether a
language model can produce evaluation data itself. AutoBencher ([LI
et al., 2025](#bib.bib69)) casts benchmark construction as an
optimization problem: a human declares desiderata such as difficulty and
salience, and a model iteratively proposes and refines dataset
descriptions that optimize surrogate metrics for them, yielding
question-answer items that elicit more model errors than
human-constructed benchmarks. A parallel line places the same
proposer-solver asymmetry inside a training loop. Self-challenging LM
agents ([Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib169)) have a single model act as a
challenger that explores a tool environment and emits tasks in a
Code-as-Task format carrying an instruction, a verification function, a
solution, and failure cases, then as an executor trained on those tasks
by RL. SPICE ([Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib75)) grounds the challenger in
a document corpus, so that the tasks it generates stay factual and sit
at the frontier of the reasoner’s ability. SPADE ([Liu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib76)) scales this to executable environments, training the
task proposer itself with a hint-based regret signal so the environment
distribution evolves as the agent improves. AutoBenchmark is closely
related to this line of work but differs in three aspects. First, our
target is autoresearch benchmarks created by autoresearch agents: the
proposer and the solvers are the same class of long-horizon agent, and
the tasks are research problems that run for hours instead of
single-turn reasoning problems. Second, the loop carries two feedback
signals. Alongside the verifiable score from the solvers’ trajectories,
an LLM verifier judges the benchmark on open-ended dimensions that no
score reveals, namely construct validity, correctness, feasibility,
usefulness, and an overall verdict. Third, we do not train the proposer.
We measure what current agents produce on their own and vary how much a
human directs them, which lets us ask which parts of benchmark creation
still need a human researcher.

Evaluating and directing autoresearch agents.  Existing benchmarks for
research agents supply the task and measure execution against it:
MLE-bench ([Chan et al., 2025](#bib.bib15)) and RE-Bench ([Wijk et al.,
2025](#bib.bib139)) score agents on machine learning engineering
problems with predefined metrics, and speedrun-style setups ([Karpathy,
2026](#bib.bib57)) fix the target and reward hill-climbing it. What
these measure is how well an agent pursues a goal someone else has set.
We ask a question one step earlier: can the agent decide what is worth
measuring and build the apparatus that measures it, a step where no
fixed procedure applies. Concurrently, work on recursive
self-improvement ([Yin et al., 2025](#bib.bib154); [Anthropic,
2026](#bib.bib5); [Weng, 2026](#bib.bib136)) asks how much of this cycle
an agent can close on its own, and co-improvement ([Weston and Foerster,
2025](#bib.bib137)) argues that the strongest and safest results still
come from agents working with human researchers. Our results speak to
both: the agents we study run the full construction loop, yet produce
near-saturated benchmarks without human direction, and the gap closes
only when that direction is specific about what to build and how to
build it.

### 1.6 Conclusion

We proposed AutoBenchmark, a pipeline which evaluates the ability of a
research agent to construct a benchmark, where we study when and how
human feedback could be useful. We particularly targeted benchmarks used
to evaluate research agents – specifically, by building Graveyard Bench,
SilentTrain Bench, and Rebuttal Bench. Our takeaway is that for current
models human feedback helps at two points, and only when it is concrete.
The first is forming the problem: a detailed specification with curated
grounding material lowered solver scores by a substantial margin, while
a one-sentence statement of intent left the benchmark close to what the
agent produced unaided. The second is supplying the way to realize it,
where guidance on how to instantiate the benchmark restarted a loop that
had stalled. Three ingredients were necessary on the agent side:
grounding material worth iterating on, feedback drawn from the solver
trajectories and the judges’ verdicts together, and a sufficient number
of loop iterations to build the benchmark.

Looking ahead, constructing high-quality challenging benchmarks is and
will be central to AI model development, and it becomes harder as the
models themselves become more capable. As recursive self-improvement
draws increasing attention, this raises the question of which parts of
benchmark construction should be delegated to agents and which should
remain with human researchers. Substantial technical work remains on the
agent side, including training the proposer to widen the proposer–solver
gap and meta-optimizing its agentic harness. The more difficult and
important question, however, concerns the human side: deciding which
problems are meaningful and worth making difficult is a judgment we do
not yet know how to delegate, and integrating it into the loop is, in
our view, the most important direction for future work. The
AutoBenchmark recipe can be used to monitor this progress as models
improve.

## 2 HackBench: Detecting and Localizing Reward Hacking in Autoresearch Agents

Figure 5: HackBench. Hack localization F₁ per model. All monitors miss
many hacks.

### 2.1 Overview

Motivation Language model agents can carry out long-horizon research
tasks end to end: given a task (“pretrain a language model with the
lowest dev perplexity,” “finetune a classifier to achieve the highest
possible accuracy”), the agent reads the codebase, writes and runs
training and evaluation code, and is scored by an automated _verifier_
([Chan et al., 2025](#bib.bib15); [Wijk et al., 2025](#bib.bib139);
[Starace et al., 2025](#bib.bib122); [Huang et al., 2024](#bib.bib45)).
However, this iterative optimization loop can be fragile. Even when the
score is computed on held-out data in a separate environment, the agent
knows, or can infer, how the score is computed: it can read the
evaluation code, inspect the test labels or test distribution, and shape
its solution to the evaluation metric rather than to the task itself.
When the objective is “make this metric go up,” an agent that did not
conduct the underlying research can still make the number go up by
_reward hacking_: exploiting a flaw in the specification to obtain
reward without accomplishing the intended task ([Skalse et al.,
2022](#bib.bib121); [Pan et al., 2022](#bib.bib102); [Weng,
2024](#bib.bib135)).

The community has highlighted the importance and difficulty of dealing
with reward hacking in autoresearch: PostTrainBench re-audited its
leaderboard after agents built training data around held-out items,
distilled from external model APIs, and submitted instruction-tuned
checkpoints in place of the assigned base model ([PostTrainBench Team,
2026](#bib.bib107)). On the NanoGPT speedrun ([Jordan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib54)), METR observed agents freezing weights or halting
training the moment the target loss was reached, and needed the
speedrun’s human maintainer to separate these brittle gains from
legitimate optimization ([Cunningham et al., 2026](#bib.bib22)). In each
case the hack is task-specific, looks like ordinary progress at the
level of individual actions, and surfaces only in long transcripts. The
cost of missing it is high: autoresearch verifiers are exactly the
reward signals used to train agents with reinforcement learning from
verifiable rewards ([DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Lightman
et al., 2024](#bib.bib73)), so a hack that survives corrupts the
training signal ([Qi et al., 2026](#bib.bib108)).

A natural research question arises: can an LLM _monitor_ catch these
hacks by reading the agent’s trajectory—i.e., can LLMs police
themselves? This task is particularly challenging: a trajectory can run
to millions of tokens, so a monitor must first exercise long-context
_memory_; the hack can be a handful of commands among hundreds (a median
of $`264`$ per trajectory in the benchmark we create in this work),
frequently buried mid-trajectory where attention is weakest ([Liu
et al., 2023](#bib.bib77); [Hsieh et al., 2024](#bib.bib44)). It must
then _reason_ across steps, because a hack is often a multi-step action
whose sub-steps are distributed through the transcript, and localization
requires identifying the exact hacking command(s) rather than merely
noticing that something is off. Finally, the monitor must bring task
_knowledge_: deciding whether a command games a grader is a scientific
judgment about the task, not a surface pattern. Unlike a synthetic
needle-in-a-haystack, the needle here cannot be found by string-matching
or by spotting an inconsistency, only by understanding the task ([Baker
et al., 2025](#bib.bib9)). Fundamentally, detection comes down to a
question of alignment with humans: even if this action can improve the
reward, is this a behavior humans would consider acceptable?

Our contribution To measure how well LLMs catch reward hacking, we build
HackBench ¹¹ 1 Dataset:
[https://huggingface.co/datasets/facebook/hackbench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/facebook/hackbench),
a benchmark for detecting and localizing reward hacks in full
autoresearch trajectories. HackBench is built from _real_ agent runs and
includes both _natural_ and _synthetic_ hacks. The _synthetic_ hacks are
long-context stress tests: covert, often multi-step hacks are injected
into long honest trajectories, and causally affected downstream
observations are patched so that the needle remains consistent with the
world state. Because we know exactly which commands were injected, these
trajectories come with ground-truth labels for scoring localization.

Using HackBench, we evaluate the following frontier proprietary models:
Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.5, Muse Spark 1.3,
and Muse Wonder, as well as the open-weight models GLM-5.2 and Kimi K3.
We find that all models fail at finding some of the hacks, so there is
still progress to be made.

Figure 6: HackBench. Given a full agent trajectory (left), an LLM
monitor (center) reads the entire transcript and is scored on the hack
localization task of returning the exact offending command(s) by command
index (right).

### 2.2 HackBench

HackBench evaluates how well an LLM monitor can detect and localize
reward hacking from a full autoresearch trajectory. It is built from
_real_ agent trajectories containing _natural_ and _synthetic_ hacks,
with audited command-level gold labels. This section formalizes the
problem and presents our taxonomy of hacks
(§[2.2.1](#S2.SS2.SSS1 "2.2.1 Problem Formulation ‣ 2.2 HackBench ‣ 2 HackBench: Detecting and Localizing Reward Hacking in Autoresearch Agents ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")),
describes the tasks and agents that produce the trajectories
(§[2.2.2](#S2.SS2.SSS2 "2.2.2 Autoresearch Grounding ‣ 2.2 HackBench ‣ 2 HackBench: Detecting and Localizing Reward Hacking in Autoresearch Agents ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")),
and details how we construct the _natural_ and _synthetic_ sets
(§[2.2.3](#S2.SS2.SSS3 "2.2.3 HackBench Construction ‣ 2.2 HackBench ‣ 2 HackBench: Detecting and Localizing Reward Hacking in Autoresearch Agents ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")).

#### 2.2.1 Problem Formulation

##### 2.2.1.1 Autoresearch tasks and trajectories.

An autoresearch task provides an agent with a working environment (code,
data, tools) and an instruction to optimize a metric. The agent
interacts with the environment over a long horizon, producing a
_trajectory_
$`\tau=(s_{0},r_{1},a_{1},o_{1},r_{2},a_{2},o_{2},\dots,r_{T},a_{T},o_{T})`$,
where $`s_{0}`$ is the initial state (the task instruction and starting
environment) and each step contributes the agent’s private reasoning
$`r_{t}`$, a command $`a_{t}`$ (keystrokes issued to a shell), and an
observation $`o_{t}`$ (terminal output). At the end, a _verifier_ $`V`$
runs in the environment and returns a scalar reward
$`R=V(\text{env}_{T})`$ computed on the final environment state
$`\text{env}_{T}`$, typically by recomputing a metric from artifacts the
agent produced.

##### 2.2.1.2 Reward hacking.

A trajectory contains _reward hacking_ if the agent obtains reward by
subverting the measurement rather than by accomplishing the task, e.g.
writing fabricated metric files, editing or monkey-patching the grader,
training or selecting on held-out test data, or reporting a subset of
results chosen to inflate the aggregate. We contrast this with
_legitimate_ work, including genuine iteration, using pretrained models,
or cutting compute while still doing the real task. The distinction is a
property of _how_ the reward was obtained, so it can only be judged from
the trajectory, not from $`R`$ alone.

##### 2.2.1.3 Monitoring.

A _monitor_ $`M`$ maps a trajectory (and optionally the task and
verifier) to a judgment about reward hacking. Specifically, we consider
monitors that output a localization of the specific command(s) that
constitute the hack.

[TABLE]

Table 2: A taxonomy of reward hacks observed in autoresearch
trajectories that we use for HackBench, grouped by scope (general vs.
task-specific), with one example per category. General hacks apply
across tasks; task-specific hacks exploit the measurement structure of a
particular task. Examples are drawn from ResearchGym and AutoLab
trajectories.

##### 2.2.1.4 Task framing.

We evaluate monitors on hack localization: each executable command is
prefixed with a \[CMD $`n`$\] index, and the monitor returns the indices
of the hacking commands. Localizing a hack in a long trajectory requires
retaining relevant context, reasoning across multiple steps, and
understanding the task and its grading procedure. HackBench therefore
also evaluates long-context reasoning in a semantically meaningful
setting.

#### 2.2.2 Autoresearch Grounding

##### 2.2.2.1 Tasks.

Our released benchmark covers 13 long-horizon ML research tasks: five
tasks from ResearchGym ([Garikaparthi et al., 2026](#bib.bib32)), seven
tasks from AutoLab’s “Model Development” subset ([Xu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib148)), and a weak-to-strong autoresearch task based on
automated-w2s-research ([Wen, 2026](#bib.bib134)). We provide detailed
descriptions of all 13 tasks in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C HackBench Task Suite ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans").

##### 2.2.2.2 Autoresearch agents.

We drive the agent with the Harbor terminus-2 scaffold ([Harbor
Framework Team, 2026](#bib.bib40)), in which the agent has access only
to a bash tool: it issues shell keystrokes and observes terminal output,
with each task running in a container. We deliberately did not use more
advanced scaffolds because our goal is not to improve autoresearch
performance; a simple terminal provides a clean testbed for studying
reward hacking. We use GPT-5.5 ([OpenAI, 2026a](#bib.bib97)) and GLM-5.2
([Z.ai, 2026](#bib.bib160)) to generate research trajectories.

#### 2.2.3 HackBench Construction

In our preliminary experiments, agents rarely hacked when the
instruction explicitly prohibited reward hacking, and the hacks we
observed covered only a few types (e.g., fabrication, cherry-picking
random seeds). Thus, while we collect naturally occurring hacks,
collecting enough across a broad range of types was impractical. We thus
developed a taxonomy of hacks
([Table 2](#S2.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 2.2.1.3 Monitoring. ‣ 2.2.1 Problem Formulation ‣ 2.2 HackBench ‣ 2 HackBench: Detecting and Localizing Reward Hacking in Autoresearch Agents ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans"))
and used it to guide synthetic hack injection into agent transcripts.
Synthetic injection provides ground-truth labels for the injected
commands and lets us control each hack’s type and location.

##### 2.2.3.1 Injecting synthetic hacks.

We construct synthetic hack trajectories in three stages
([Figure 7](#S2.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 2.2.3.2 Collecting natural hacks. ‣ 2.2.3 HackBench Construction ‣ 2.2 HackBench ‣ 2 HackBench: Detecting and Localizing Reward Hacking in Autoresearch Agents ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")).
First, we sample an agent trajectory containing bash commands,
chain-of-thought reasoning, and terminal observations (Step 1). Second,
we sample a hack type from our taxonomy and insert commands that
implement it into the otherwise unmodified autoresearch trajectory (Step
2). Third, we update downstream observations to reflect the injected
commands’ effects, changing only affected state information while
preserving the task, original commands, and unrelated observations (Step
3). We used GLM-5.2 to perform both command injection and observation
updates. We then used Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 to audit each
trajectory to check whether the injected commands constitute reward
hacking and whether downstream observations are consistent with the
injection. We manually annotated cases where the two auditors disagreed.

##### 2.2.3.2 Collecting natural hacks.

To surface candidates for naturally occurring hacks, we used GPT-5.6 Sol
to screen autoresearch trajectories, dividing each transcript into eight
chunks. We selected this configuration based on a pilot study of
transcript screening, in which it achieved the highest recall among the
configurations we tested.

After human auditing, we combined 41 trajectories containing natural
hacks with 128 trajectories containing synthetic hacks to form
HackBench, a benchmark of 169 reward-hacking trajectories.

[Table 3](#S2.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 2.2.3.2 Collecting natural hacks. ‣ 2.2.3 HackBench Construction ‣ 2.2 HackBench ‣ 2 HackBench: Detecting and Localizing Reward Hacking in Autoresearch Agents ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")characterizes
the resulting benchmark’s scale and sparsity. Trajectories have a median
length of over one million characters and a median of 264 commands, yet
the median number of gold-labeled hacking commands is only one. The
median per-trajectory share of hacking commands is just 0.6%, requiring
monitors to locate sparse evidence within long research histories.
Nevertheless, some trajectories contain many hacking commands (up to
383), so the benchmark covers both isolated actions and multi-command
cases.

### 2.3 Hack Localization Results

We evaluate LLM monitors on hack localization in HackBench. Each command
block in a trajectory is assigned a \[CMD $`n`$\] index, and the monitor
predicts the set of indices corresponding to hacking commands. Gold
indices are aligned with the same preprocessed transcript shown to the
monitor.

We report three metrics: precision, the fraction of predicted hacking
commands that belong to the gold set; recall, the fraction of gold
hacking commands recovered by the monitor; and F₁, the harmonic mean of
precision and recall. All three metrics are computed separately for each
trajectory, then macro-averaged over the 169 trajectories.

|                 |                    |                    |                    |

[Table 4](#S2.T4 "In 2.3 Hack Localization Results ‣ 2 HackBench: Detecting and Localizing Reward Hacking in Autoresearch Agents ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
reports hack localization performance across models. Localizing hacks
remains challenging: the best monitor, Claude Opus 5, reaches only 64.88
F₁, followed by Muse Wonder at 61.47; every other model stays below 53.
Four models (GPT-5.6 Sol, Kimi K3, Claude Opus 4.8, and GPT-5.5) cluster

trade-offs; for example, GPT-5.6 Sol attains the second-highest recall
(68.55) but over-flags, with a precision of only 54.84.

### 2.4 Related Work

##### Reward hacking and specification gaming.

Reward hacking—high reward without the intended behavior—is a
long-standing concern in reinforcement learning ([Amodei et al.,
2016](#bib.bib4); [Krakovna et al., 2020](#bib.bib64); [Skalse et al.,
2022](#bib.bib121); [Pan et al., 2022](#bib.bib102); [Manheim and
Garrabrant, 2018](#bib.bib84)). In the RLHF/RLVR era it reappears as
reward-model overoptimization ([Gao et al., 2022](#bib.bib31);
[Moskovitz et al., 2023](#bib.bib90); [Eisenstein et al.,
2024](#bib.bib27)) and, more sharply, as _reward tampering_, where a
model edits its own reward channel ([Denison et al., 2024](#bib.bib24)).
We study reward hacking in a setting where the “reward” is a concrete
automated verifier the agent can read and modify, and where hacks are
often multi-step programs rather than single actions.

##### Autonomous research agents.

Agentic coding and tool use ([Yao et al., 2022](#bib.bib152); [Schick
et al., 2023](#bib.bib117); [Jimenez et al., 2024](#bib.bib51); [Yang
et al., 2024b](#bib.bib150)) now extend to end-to-end ML research, and a
wave of benchmarks measures it: MLE-bench ([Chan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib15)), RE-Bench ([Wijk et al., 2025](#bib.bib139)),
PaperBench ([Starace et al., 2025](#bib.bib122)), MLAgentBench ([Huang
et al., 2024](#bib.bib45)), ResearchGym ([Garikaparthi et al.,
2026](#bib.bib32)), MLS-Bench ([Lyu et al., 2026](#bib.bib81)), and
AutoLab ([Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib148)). These works optimize for and
measure _capability_. We instead treat their tasks as a testbed in which
to study _integrity_: the same open-ended, verifier-scored task that
measures research skill also invites hacking of the verifier. Closely
related to our work, [Huang et al. (2026)](#bib.bib46) studies when
reward hacking occurs and what forms it takes. Our work complements
[Huang et al. (2026)](#bib.bib46) by studying how well
language-model-based monitors detect and locate reward hacking in
autoresearch transcripts.

##### Oversight, monitoring, and control.

Detecting misbehavior from a model’s behavior or reasoning is central to
scalable oversight ([Bowman et al., 2022](#bib.bib13)), weak-to-strong
generalization ([Burns et al., 2023](#bib.bib14)), and AI control
([Greenblatt et al., 2024](#bib.bib36)). Chain-of-thought monitoring can
catch reward hacking but is fragile if optimized against ([Baker et al.,
2025](#bib.bib9)), and reasoning traces are not always faithful ([Turpin
et al., 2023](#bib.bib127)); frontier models can scheme and hide intent
when incentivized ([Meinke et al., 2024](#bib.bib87); [Hubinger et al.,
2024](#bib.bib47)). To monitor agents, [Kutasov et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib66) propose asking agents to perform both a main task
and a covert side task in general agentic settings (e.g., booking an
airplane ticket), then checking whether monitors catch the side task.
[Libon et al. (2026)](#bib.bib72) extends the main/side task red-teaming
protocol to autoresearch settings. For coding agents, [Deshpande et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib25) benchmark reward-hack detection in code environments
via contrastive analysis. However, [Martin and Roger (2026)](#bib.bib85)
and [Jotautaitė et al. (2026)](#bib.bib55) find that existing monitoring
benchmarks may overestimate monitor performance because they evaluate
monitors on relatively short trajectories and a narrow range of hacks.
In our work, we mitigate these limitations through injection-based
red-teaming: directly asking a model to inject different hack commands
into long agent transcripts.

##### LLM judges and long context.

We build on LLM-as-a-judge methods ([Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib166);
[Li et al., 2023](#bib.bib70); [Dubois et al., 2024](#bib.bib26)), using
LLMs to assess whether agent trajectories contain reward hacking.
Because these trajectories can be very long, monitoring is subject to
known failure modes such as lost-in-the-middle effects and
context-window limits ([Liu et al., 2023](#bib.bib77); [Hsieh et al.,
2024](#bib.bib44)).

### 2.5 Conclusion

Autoresearch agents reward-hack because we ask them to maximize metrics,
and they do so without proper regard to other implicit constraints, i.e.
they should also perform actions humans would consider acceptable. We
thus built HackBench, a benchmark that measures whether hacks inside
autoresearch trajectories can be detected and localized, and showed that
current frontier models do not fully succeed at this task. As agents
take on more of the research loop, monitoring reward hacking is not an
add-on but a prerequisite; to support future work, we release
trajectories containing naturally occurring and synthetically injected
hacks, together with audited command-level gold labels.

## 3 Training agents to interact with humans

### 3.1 Overview

Motivation Today, AI models are routinely used by humans for coding and
research, and further progress in their ability to interact with us
increasingly depends on the data and environments they are trained on.
However, the most common post-training recipe trains on fully specified
tasks paired with an automatic verifier, with no human in the loop –
which aligns with the fully automatic autoresearch ([Karpathy,
2026](#bib.bib57)) paradigm. This creates a major discrepancy with
real-world applications where agents work with users by following
clarifications and feedback ([Jin et al., 2025](#bib.bib52); [Wang
et al., 2026](#bib.bib132)). While current training tasks are usually
fully specified, users in reality are much less specific. They may start
with a goal that is not fully articulated, provide clarifications after
seeing the agent’s output, revise requests midway, or provide
counterexamples when a fix does not hold ([Baumann et al.,
2026](#bib.bib11); [Wu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib144)). Models that solve
tasks without such context can lose track of intent as the interaction
goes on ([Laban et al., 2026](#bib.bib68); [Tack et al.,
2026](#bib.bib124)).

An obvious direction is thus to train models to be better at agent-human
interactions. However, common training recipes are not designed for an
interactive setup: real interaction logs are scarce, costly, and
difficult to convert into verifiable training examples ([Baumann et al.,
2026](#bib.bib11)). An alternative is to simulate interactions, but
these can be miscalibrated against real user behavior or collapse a
heterogeneous user population onto a generic persona ([Cheng et al.,
2023](#bib.bib17)). Moreover, ensuring task diversity, factual
grounding, and executable verification in synthesized interactions is
itself not straightforward. The problem for synthetic data is therefore
to construct interaction data that is realistic, grounded in verifiable
tasks with high-quality reference solutions, and calibrated in
difficulty to the model being trained.

Our contribution We introduce AutoInteract, a framework for generating
data to train agents to interact with humans. Inspired by the recent
Autodata method ([Kulikov et al., 2026](#bib.bib65)), which uses an
agentic data scientist to create high-quality synthetic data,
AutoInteract generalizes that approach to treat human-agent interaction
itself as the object of synthesis. Starting from a verified source task,
our method simulates a multi-turn interaction, including user
clarifications, requirement changes, and corrective feedback, while
preserving the source task’s final reference solution verifiable by an
executable test. This consists of two phases: (1) creating user models
from real interaction histories by learning behavior over a diverse
population of profiles and (2) combining these user models with
problem-solving agents in an agentic generate–evaluate–revise loop that
simulates realistic, task-grounded interactions with calibrated
difficulty for a given model. Models can then be trained with
reinforcement learning on this data.

Across algorithmic coding and software engineering tasks, AutoInteract
substantially outperforms baselines with both Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-27B
backbones. On LiveCodeBench-Pro ([Zheng et al., 2026](#bib.bib167)) and
its multi-turn variant, AutoInteract raises average Pass@1 from $`29.9`$
to $`43.0`$ at 4B and from $`49.1`$ to $`55.7`$ at 27B, with especially
large multi-turn gains from $`23.0`$ to $`43.2`$ and from $`37.2`$ to
$`50.6`$, respectively. On SWE-Together ([Wu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib144)), it improves Pass@1 from $`6.0`$ to $`20.6`$ at 4B
and from $`34.9`$ to $`38.5`$ at 27B. Our analysis shows that multi-turn
synthesis, grounded user models, and executable verification each
contribute to performance, while training reward does not saturate as
quickly as training on the source data.

Overall, our results show that training can extend beyond solving
isolated tasks to help models learn how to work with users. By making
interaction itself synthesizable and verifiable, AutoInteract provides a
practical way to train agents to incorporate human clarifications,
feedback, and evolving requirements while still optimizing for task
correctness.

### 3.2 AutoInteract

![Refer to caption](2610.38882v1/autointeract_refined.png)

Figure 8: AutoInteract is a two-phase framework for generating
realistic, high-quality multi-turn interaction trajectories from
verified tasks based on real user histories. In Phase 1, AutoInteract
builds user models: modeling how users react by optimizing a
history-conditioned user behavior prompt and building a diverse set of
user profiles. In Phase 2, an agent combines verified source tasks with
its user models to generate candidate tasks with multi-turn interaction
trajectories, and selects them to be challenging, valid, realistic,
coherent, and profile-consistent. If the checks fail, it revises the
controller’s instruction until a task passes all checks or the retry
budget is exhausted.

AutoInteract is a framework for generating user-centric interaction
training and evaluation data. It produces realistic, verifiable,
multi-turn tasks between a simulated user and an assistant. Because
these trajectories resemble the interactions that assistants encounter
in practice, models can learn from them to better handle real
user-centric tasks.

AutoInteract first learns a user model from logged interactions, so
simulated users reproduce the habits, gaps, and preferences that real
users show. The pipeline needs only raw interaction logs with user IDs,
so it carries over to any domain where such logs exist.

AutoInteract then performs task-grounded trajectory synthesis, which
preserves the source task’s existing reference solution and executable
verifier. The user simulator privately conditions on the reference
solution and executable checks to keep requests across turns consistent
with the original task, without revealing this privileged information to
the assistant. The final assistant response can therefore be scored by
the source task’s unchanged verifier.

The method thus runs in two phases, shown in
Figure [8](#S3.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 3.2 AutoInteract ‣ 3 Training agents to interact with humans ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans").
Phase 1 builds user models from real histories so that we can simulate
users realistically. A user model has two parts: (1) a user behavior
prompt, which gives general role-playing behavior guidance, and (2) a
user profile, which describes the specific user being simulated. We
learn both using an existing corpus of real trajectories of users
interacting with coding agents. We learn the user behavior prompt using
GEPA ([Agrawal et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)), guided by reference-based
feedback that measures how closely a simulated next turn matches real
user behavior in the same conversation context. We then build a set of
user profiles by using an LLM to summarize user traits from the
histories, including diversification and validation steps. Together, the
user behavior prompt and the user profiles let us simulate users.
Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Building User Models from Real Histories ‣ 3 Training agents to interact with humans ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
provides more details.

Phase 2 builds interaction trajectories with an agent controlling the
user simulation inside a loop that generates, evaluates, and improves
trajectories. A controller starts each trajectory-synthesis process by
picking a verified source task, pairing it with a user model from Phase
1, and planning how the interaction should unfold. It passes this plan
as an instruction to a trajectory generator, where the user simulator
(using the user model) and an assistant simulator talk over multiple
turns to produce a candidate trajectory. A trajectory evaluator then
checks the result on three axes: whether the task is valid and free of
leakage, whether the interaction is realistic and coherent, and whether
the difficulty is appropriately calibrated, so that a weak solver
struggles while a strong solver succeeds. Trajectories that pass are
kept as training data. Trajectories that fail go back to the controller,
which reflects on the failure, revises the instruction, and retries.
Section [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Building Interactions with an Agentic Loop ‣ 3 Training agents to interact with humans ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
provides more details.

Figure 9: The user-simulator prompt used to generate each user turn. It
combines the learned user behavior prompt and a sampled user profile
from Phase 1 with the interaction history and the privileged task
context. After a failed attempt, the controller may also add revised
role-playing guidance based on the trajectory evaluator’s feedback.

### 3.3 Building User Models from Real Histories

Phase 1 builds user models from real interaction histories. Each user
model has two parts: (1) a user behavior prompt, which gives general
role-playing guidance on how users tend to react, and (2) a user
profile, which describes the specific user being simulated. We learn
both components from real data of users interacting with agents. The
user behavior prompt is optimized on observed next-user turns, while the
profile population is built from (LLM-generated summaries of) behavior
across users, diversified, and validated. Together, these two parts
determine how a simulated user responds and the interaction style they
follow.
Appendix [F.1](#A6.SS1 "F.1 Implementation Details for Building User Models from Real Histories ‣ Appendix F AutoInteract Implementation Details ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
provides further implementation details beyond this section.

#### 3.3.1 Optimizing a History-Conditioned User Behavior Prompt

The user behavior prompt is a reusable set of instructions for
role-playing a human developer. It defines the simulator’s role and
output format, explains how to use the conversation history and user
profile, and describes common user reactions, such as accepting the
work, correcting the assistant, reporting a failure, changing a
requirement, or ending the interaction. It also asks the simulator to
keep follow-up messages short and grounded in the current conversation.
The prompt does not describe a specific task or user. To simulate users
during trajectory synthesis, we combine it with a sampled user profile,
the interaction history, and the source task as private context to the
user simulator
(Figure [9](#S3.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ 3.2 AutoInteract ‣ 3 Training agents to interact with humans ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")).

We optimize a single user behavior prompt while keeping the simulator’s
model weights fixed. We instantiate GEPA ([Agrawal et al.,
2026](#bib.bib3)), a reflective prompt optimizer that evolves prompts
using natural-language evaluation feedback and Pareto-based candidate
selection. Each training instance contains a conversation prefix, an
assigned user profile, and the real user’s next message. Given the
prefix and persona, a candidate user behavior prompt generates a
simulated next message. An LLM evaluator assigns an overall score based
on intent, reaction to the assistant, length, specificity, persona
consistency, and realism, and provides textual feedback describing
discrepancies from the real turn. For each sampled training minibatch,
GEPA uses this feedback to propose a revised user behavior prompt and
accepts the revision when it improves the minibatch score. Accepted
candidates are evaluated on the validation set to update the
per-instance Pareto frontier, and the final user behavior prompt is
selected by aggregate validation performance.

#### 3.3.2 Constructing a Behavior-Grounded Profile Population

We build the user profile population in three steps: build (prompt an
LLM to summarize) one profile from each real user’s history, diversify
these profiles while preserving their interaction patterns, and validate
the resulting population. LLMs write and audit the profile text, while
behavioral structure and population-level validation use automated,
data-driven procedures.

Profile construction. For each user ID recorded in the user source data,
we aggregate that user’s conversations and compute a profile summary,
including what kinds of requests they make, how often they correct or
push back on the assistant, how often their requirements change, and how
much detail they provide. We prompt an LLM to summarize this evidence
into a concise natural-language profile (see the prompt in
Box [F.1](#A6.SS1 "F.1 Implementation Details for Building User Models from Real Histories ‣ Appendix F AutoInteract Implementation Details ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")).
This profile tells the simulator how the user tends to behave across
turns, including user vagueness, pushback, requirement changes,
verbosity, and the rate at which requirements are revealed across the
conversation.

Profile diversification. The observed users do not provide enough
profiles for large-scale simulation, so we develop a method inspired by
MAP-Elites ([Mouret and Clune, 2015](#bib.bib91)), a quality-diversity
method that expands coverage across behavioral types/clusters (also
called niches or cells) while retaining high-quality profiles in each
type. Clusters are defined by expertise, vagueness, pushback,
requirement-change tendency, and verbosity, and only combinations found
among real users are kept. Within each cluster, we prompt an LLM to
write new profiles that preserve a real user’s behavior settings and
tone while varying surface details. The settings are inherited from the
real profiles, adding diversity without inventing unsupported behavior
combinations.

Profile validation. Profiles are validated for quality. We employ an LLM
to check each generated profile against the user’s measured fingerprint,
flag unsupported claims and repository-specific details, and provide
feedback for revision. During verification, automatic text-similarity
checks remove near-duplicates and profiles that are unusually far from
all real profiles. Final automatic checks measure behavioral-type
coverage, diversity, and distributional similarity to the real users
from the source data.

### 3.4 Building Interactions with an Agentic Loop

Phase 2 turns verified source tasks combined with the user models from
Phase 1 into realistic, verifiable tasks with multi-turn trajectories.
As shown in
Figure [8](#S3.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 3.2 AutoInteract ‣ 3 Training agents to interact with humans ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
(right), the agentic loop consists of three modules:

1.  (1)
    Controller, which samples a verified source task and user profile
    and uses them, together with the learned user-behavior prompt, to
    specify the scenario and guide the conversation. After a failed
    attempt, it revises these instructions using evaluator feedback.
2.  (2)
    Trajectory generator, which follows the controller’s instruction and
    rolls out a candidate conversation between the user simulator and
    the assistant simulator.
3.  (3)
    Trajectory evaluator, which checks the candidate for validity and
    leakage, realism and coherence, profile consistency, and difficulty
    calibrated through solver rollouts and the source task’s executable
    verifier.

Together, these modules form a data generation loop: the controller
proposes an interaction, the generator produces it, and the evaluator
determines whether to keep it or return it for revision.

#### 3.4.1 Interaction Task Synthesis (Controller + Trajectory generator)

Each trajectory begins with a verified source task. The controller pairs
the task with the learned user behavior prompt and a sampled profile and
generates an initial plan. The plan is a natural-language instruction
that defines the user’s goal, behavior, information-disclosure strategy,
and how the conversation progresses; see
Box [F.2](#A6.SS2 "F.2 Implementation Details for Building Interactions with an Agentic Loop ‣ Appendix F AutoInteract Implementation Details ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
for an example. At each turn, the user simulator receives the
user-simulation prompt shown in
Figure [9](#S3.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ 3.2 AutoInteract ‣ 3 Training agents to interact with humans ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans"),
which combines these two components of the user model with the visible
interaction history, the source task and reference information as a
privileged context, and any revised controller guidance from a previous
failed attempt. The assistant simulator responds only to the
conversation and any repository context it would normally observe. The
conversation ends on a user turn, and the requirements expressed across
the interaction aim to remain verifiable with the source task’s original
verifier.

Scenario-guided algorithmic trajectories. For self-contained algorithmic
tasks, the controller follows several interaction patterns, detailed in
its generated plan: clarification or requirement change during design,
clarification or requirement change after an initial solution, and bug
iteration through concrete failing cases. Clarification reveals a
requirement that was present from the start, a requirement change
introduces a genuinely new need, and bug iteration keeps the
specification fixed. These patterns control when information becomes
visible without changing the final verified task.

History-conditioned repository trajectories. Repository-level software
engineering tasks are more agentic than self-contained algorithmic
tasks, requiring tool-driven repository search, fault localization,
editing, testing, and responses to users across turns. The interaction
is shaped by the user behavior prompt and sampled profile. Private task
and reference information keep the simulated user factually grounded,
while the assistant operates only on the visible conversation and
repository state. The cumulative user requests must describe the
intended change without revealing private tests or implementation
details.
Appendix [F.3](#A6.SS3 "F.3 Details of Training Tasks ‣ Appendix F AutoInteract Implementation Details ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
provides further details on both task regimes.

#### 3.4.2 Agentic Self-Improvement

Initial generation does not guarantee that a trajectory is realistic,
valid, or useful for training. Like Autodata’s agentic data scientist,
which improves synthetic data through solver and judge feedback
([Kulikov et al., 2026](#bib.bib65)), AutoInteract repeatedly generates,
evaluates, and revises candidates, but focuses the improvement process
on multi-turn trajectories with a user (model) and grounds it in
executable verification.

Multi-objective trajectory evaluation. The evaluator checks three
properties: the task is valid and does not leak private information; the
interaction is realistic, coherent, and consistent with the sampled
profile; and the difficulty is calibrated so that the target model
struggles while a stronger solver succeeds. Solver responses are scored
with the source task’s executable verifier. This combines semantic
checks with execution-based evidence, and a trajectory is kept only when
all checks pass.

Trajectory self-reflection. When a check fails, the evaluator identifies
whether the trajectory is invalid, unrealistic, inconsistent with the
profile, too easy for the target model, too difficult for the stronger
solver, or overly revealing. The controller turns this diagnosis into
guidance for the next rollout. The source task, learned user behavior
prompt, and sampled profile remain fixed across attempts, so the
controller revises only the task interaction. This
generate–evaluate–revise loop continues until the trajectory passes or
the retry budget is exhausted.

### 3.5 Experimental Setup

#### 3.5.1 Training Setup

User Model Data. We learn the user behavior prompt and user profiles
from SWE-Chat ([Baumann et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)), a corpus of real
trajectories of users interacting with coding agents, where each
trajectory records a user ID and how that user responds in different
situations.

Source Data. For algorithmic coding, we extract the code subset of
Dolci-Think-RL-32B, the reinforcement-learning corpus used to train
OLMo 3 ([Olmo et al., 2025](#bib.bib95)). Our extraction contains 12,120
Python problems, each represented by a natural-language specification
and a list of executable assertions that serve as its ground-truth
verifier. For repository-level SWE, we use SWE-smith ([Yang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib151)). Each instance provides an issue-style problem
statement, a reproducible buggy repository state, relevant code context,
an executable environment, tests that must change from failing to
passing, and regression tests that must remain passing. We construct a
deterministic pool of 19,000 function-level, pytest-backed instances
across 117 repository environments, prioritizing compact fixes with
bounded test suites.

Data Generation Configuration. In Phase 1, Kimi-K2.6 ([Kimi Team,
2025](#bib.bib62)) is used throughout user-model construction. For user
behavior prompt learning, it simulates and judges next-user turns and
performs GEPA prompt rewriting; for user-profile construction, it
drafts, expands, reformats, and verifies the profiles. In Phase 2,
Kimi-K2.6 serves as the user simulator, controller, trajectory
evaluator, and strong solver, while the target model itself serves as
the assistant simulator and weak solver: Qwen3.5-4B when generating data
for the 4B-scale runs and Qwen3.5-27B for the 27B-scale runs. Data are
therefore synthesized separately for each target scale, so the
difficulty band is calibrated to the model that will be trained on it.
For each candidate trajectory, the weak and strong solvers each generate
three responses, which are scored by the source task’s executable
verifier. A trajectory passes only when the weak solver scores at most
$`40\%`$ and the strong solver scores at least $`70\%`$; failed
candidates may undergo up to five self-improvement rounds.

Training Configuration. Each synthesized trajectory becomes a training
prompt ending on the final user turn, and the model generates only the
final assistant response. Rewards come from the source task’s executable
verification: for algorithmic tasks, the reward is the fraction of
assertions passed; for SWE tasks, it is the fraction of previously
failing tests fixed, with reward set to zero if any previously passing
test regresses. Both rewards lie in $`[0,1]`$. We train all RL variants
using the prime-rl framework ([Intellect, 2025](#bib.bib48)) with a
DAPO-style group-relative objective ([Yu et al., 2026](#bib.bib156)),
using 32 prompts and $`G=8`$ responses per prompt, for 256 responses per
update. Training uses temperature 1.0, reasoning enabled, a maximum
sequence length of 81,920 tokens, and AdamW with a constant learning
rate of $`1\times 10^{-6}`$, weight decay 0.01, gradient-norm clipping
at 1.0, and up to 500 steps.

#### 3.5.2 Evaluation Setup

Models and Baselines. We use Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-27B as the target
models throughout and compare AutoInteract against two baselines: (1)
Base, the off-the-shelf post-trained checkpoint at each scale without
further optimization, which establishes the starting performance; and
(2) RL on Source Data, which applies reinforcement learning directly to
the single-turn source data. RL on Source Data and AutoInteract use the
same source data and training configuration described in
Section [3.5.1](#S3.SS5.SSS1 "3.5.1 Training Setup ‣ 3.5 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Training agents to interact with humans ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans").

Evaluation Benchmarks. For algorithmic coding, we first evaluate on
LiveCodeBench-Pro ([Zheng et al., 2026](#bib.bib167)), a challenging
benchmark for competitive programming. We use all 706 tasks with
executable test cases: 391 easy, 251 medium, and 64 hard Codeforces
problems. Models produce C++ solutions, which are scored by exact
acceptance under the benchmark’s test cases and original time and memory
limits. We additionally construct Multi-turn LiveCodeBench-Pro from the
same task pool to isolate interaction-following ability from underlying
problem difficulty. For each source problem, we generate a conversation
using one of the five interaction scenarios in
Section [3.4.1](#S3.SS4.SSS1 "3.4.1 Interaction Task Synthesis (Controller + Trajectory generator) ‣ 3.4 Building Interactions with an Agentic Loop ‣ 3 Training agents to interact with humans ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
and retain only conversations that pass validity and realism checks. The
original problem identity and test suite are preserved, so the final C++
response is judged by the unchanged LiveCodeBench-Pro verifier. For
repository-level SWE, we use SWE-Together ([Wu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib144)), a benchmark of 109 sandboxed repository tasks
reconstructed from real user–agent sessions. Its reactive user simulator
continues the interaction according to the original user’s intent,
allowing evaluation of both task correctness and how much corrective
effort the user must provide. See [Wu et al. (2026b)](#bib.bib144) or
[Table 6](#S3.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 3.5.2 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3.5 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Training agents to interact with humans ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
for the metrics that are used.
