### 3.6 Experimental Results

#### 3.6.1 Main Results

Our main results are given in
Table [5](#S3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 3.5.2 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3.5 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Training agents to interact with humans ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
for LiveCodeBench-Pro and Multi-turn LiveCodeBench-Pro and
Table [6](#S3.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 3.5.2 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3.5 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Training agents to interact with humans ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
for SWE-Together. Our findings are summarized below.

Grounded multi-turn data improves interactive coding at both scales,
without losing single-turn ability.  At the 4B scale, AutoInteract
reaches an average of $`43.0`$: $`+13.1`$ over the baseline performance
and $`+6.1`$ over RL on the original source tasks
(Table [5](#S3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 3.5.2 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3.5 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Training agents to interact with humans ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")).
At the 27B scale, it reaches $`55.7`$: $`+6.6`$ over the baseline
performance and $`+6.1`$ over source-task training, where the latter
only improves over the initial baseline by $`+0.5`$. Our method achieves
particularly large gains on Multi-turn LiveCodeBench-Pro, where the
model must recover a specification that arrives over several turns:
$`23.0\rightarrow 43.2`$ at 4B scale and $`37.2\rightarrow 50.6`$ at 27B
scale. These gains do not come from specializing for conversation:
although AutoInteract trains on multi-turn trajectories, single-turn
LiveCodeBench-Pro rises in parallel at 4B scale from $`36.8`$ to
$`42.8`$, whereas training on the same tasks in their original
single-turn form leaves it flat ($`37.1`$), while at 27B it remains
essentially unchanged ($`60.9\rightarrow 60.8`$). Gains are on easy and
medium problems; hard Codeforces tasks remain out of reach at both
scales for all methods.

Real-user-grounded interaction data improves repository-level issue
resolution.  On SWE-Together at 4B, AutoInteract raises Pass@1 from
$`6.0`$ to $`20.6`$ and SSR from $`1.8`$ to $`16.5`$, outperforming RL
on the source tasks by 3.6 points on Pass@1 and 5.5 points on SSR
(Table [6](#S3.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 3.5.2 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3.5 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Training agents to interact with humans ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans"),
see caption for metric definitions). Consistency improves alongside
accuracy: Pass² and mean judge score both increase, indicating that
solved sessions are reproduced rather than won once by chance. At the
27B scale, AutoInteract is the only method that improves Pass@1
($`34.9\rightarrow 38.5`$), and it adds $`7.3`$ points of SSR, whereas
RL on the source tasks regresses to $`27.1`$. The interaction also
becomes cheaper for the user: at the 4B scale, AutoInteract needs fewer
corrections than the source-data run ($`6.58`$ vs. $`6.73`$) while
solving more tasks, with $`69.2`$k tokens and $`25.1`$ minutes per task
against $`73.7`$k and $`39.7`$, and at 27B it is the fastest
configuration ($`19.5`$ vs. $`32.2`$ and $`52.1`$ minutes) at the cost
of slightly more corrections ($`3.44`$ vs. $`2.91`$). The baseline’s low
U-Corr at 4B scale ($`3.78`$) is not evidence of efficiency, since it
abandons most sessions early at $`6.0`$ Pass@1.

without revealing the solution. The final trajectory is accepted with
weak- and strong-solver scores of $`25\%`$ and $`100\%`$ and passes all
validity, leakage, and realism checks.

#### 3.6.2 Ablations

Multi-turn training data is key to learning how to work with users.  The
_w/o multi-turn_ variant uses the learned user models and executable
verification but presents each task in a single turn without simulating
a multi-turn interaction between the user and assistant. This lowers
average performance from $`34.0`$ to $`28.2`$, driven primarily by the
drop on Multi-turn LiveCodeBench-Pro ($`43.2\rightarrow 29.2`$;
Table [7](#S3.T7 "Table 7 ‣ 3.6.1 Main Results ‣ 3.6 Experimental Results ‣ 3 Training agents to interact with humans ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")).
Training on interactions with user clarifications, feedback, and
evolving requirements is therefore necessary for learning to incorporate
information across turns and drives higher performance in multi-turn
interaction settings.

User models learned from real histories prepare models for diverse
users.  The _w/o user models_ variant uses multi-turn synthesis and
executable verification but relies on the initial, fixed user behavior
prompt without optimization against real-user interactions and omits the
diverse user profiles. Average performance falls from $`34.0`$ to
$`32.0`$, with the clearest degradation in SWE-Together reliability
(SSR: $`16.5\rightarrow 12.8`$). Learning both general user behavior and
user-specific variation from real histories produces training
interactions that better prepare models to adapt to how real users
behave and to differences among users.

Executable verification is critical for reliable data selection.  The
_w/o executable verification_ variant uses multi-turn synthesis and the
learned user models but relies on an LLM judge to assess solver answers
and screen task validity without executing the answers against the
verifier. Average performance falls from $`34.0`$ to $`25.0`$, similar
to _w/o all components_ at $`24.7`$
(Table [7](#S3.T7 "Table 7 ‣ 3.6.1 Main Results ‣ 3.6 Experimental Results ‣ 3 Training agents to interact with humans ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")).
Executable verification is necessary both to evaluate the weak and
strong solvers correctly for difficulty calibration and to provide a
reliable signal for correctness and validity that catches invalid
synthesized problems an LLM judge can miss.

#### 3.6.3 Analysis

Self-improvement rounds make the data more useful and increase data
yield. AutoInteract’s agentic trajectory self-improvement revises each
failed trajectory for up to five rounds, using evaluator feedback to
target its failures. Across self-improvement rounds, the fraction of
trajectories in the 4B-scale data pool that are accepted by the
trajectory evaluator increases from 9.4% after initial generation to
28.1% after five revision rounds for algorithmic tasks, and from 26.6%
to 50.9% for SWE tasks. Revisions supply $`52.4\%`$ of accepted
trajectories; $`85.5\%`$ of recovered SWE trajectories arrive in the
first two rounds, while algorithmic gains span all five. Initial
failures differ by domain: $`83.2\%`$ of algorithmic candidates are too
easy, while $`35.3\%`$ of SWE candidates leak implementation details and
$`22.2\%`$ remain too hard for the strong solver. The loop uses
additional inference compute to address each trajectory’s failure and
perform domain-specific calibration. These rounds produce high-quality
trajectories at the target difficulty, and training on AutoInteract
trajectories does not saturate as quickly as source-task training,
eventually reaching higher reward in both domains
(Figure [10](#S3.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ 3.6.1 Main Results ‣ 3.6 Experimental Results ‣ 3 Training agents to interact with humans ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")).

Trajectory self-improvement adjusts how and when task information is
revealed.
Figure [11](#S3.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ 3.6.1 Main Results ‣ 3.6 Experimental Results ‣ 3 Training agents to interact with humans ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
illustrates this effect with one example. The source task, learned user
behavior prompt, and sampled profile remain fixed, so solver outcomes
reflect only how the task turns are built. Stage 1 gives away the likely
code change and fails the weak-solver difficulty constraint. Stage 2
removes that clue but withholds needed evidence, falling below the
strong-solver solvability target. Stage 3 restores the example file,
expected behavior, and follow-up requirements without exposing the
solution, yielding weak- and strong-solver scores of $`25\%`$ and
$`100\%`$ and passing every quality check. Together, these targeted
revisions turn a rejected trajectory into useful training data without
changing its underlying task. The loop therefore does not uniformly make
tasks harder; it adjusts what is revealed and when to balance
difficulty, solvability, grounding, and realism.

### 3.7 Related Work

User Simulation. Simulated users have long been used in interactive
systems, from agenda-based simulators for training dialogue policies
([Schatzmann et al., 2007](#bib.bib116)) to populations of generative
agents that model human behavior at scale ([Park et al.,
2023](#bib.bib104)). LLMs have made user simulators more fluent and
general, and they are now widely used in interactive agent benchmarks
([Yao et al., 2024](#bib.bib153); [Barres et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)) and
as environments for training agents. Yet these simulators may not behave
like real users. Assistant-tuned models prompted to play a user often
produce turns that are unusually cooperative, well-organized, and
similar in style, and stronger assistants can make _worse_ simulators
([Naous et al., 2026](#bib.bib93)). Conditioning on a persona label can
also represent a group through stereotypes rather than the variation
found among real users ([Cheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib17)). Recent work
addresses this problem by training simulators on real interactions,
either through supervised learning on observed user turns ([Naous
et al., 2026](#bib.bib93)) or reinforcement learning for persona
consistency ([Abdulhai et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)) and latent user states
([Wu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib143); [Jin et al., 2026](#bib.bib53)). Large
persona libraries provide another way to represent diverse users ([Ge
et al., 2024](#bib.bib33)). AutoInteract combines these directions.
Rather than updating model weights or drawing profiles from an
open-ended persona library, it learns an editable user behavior prompt
from real interactions and builds a profile population from measured
per-user behavior.

Multi-Turn Interaction Evaluation and Training. Models that solve fully
specified tasks often perform worse when the same information arrives
over several turns ([Laban et al., 2026](#bib.bib68)) or when the goal
changes during a conversation ([Tack et al., 2026](#bib.bib124)).
Single-turn evaluation does not capture this problem. Interactive
benchmarks test it through feedback and tool loops ([Wang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib129)), dual-control settings ([Barres et al.,
2025](#bib.bib10)), preference-elicitation environments ([Qian et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib109)), and repository sessions reconstructed from real
developer–agent transcripts ([Baumann et al., 2026](#bib.bib11); [Wu
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib144)). Several training methods place a simulated
user in the optimization loop: SWEET-RL learns turn-level advantages
from privileged training information ([Zhou et al., 2025](#bib.bib168));
CollabLLM estimates the long-term value of a reply by sampling future
conversations ([Wu et al., 2025](#bib.bib142)); UserRL studies turn- and
trajectory-level rewards across user-centered environments ([Qian
et al., 2025b](#bib.bib110)); and MUA-RL trains multi-turn tool use with
an LLM user ([Zhao et al., 2025](#bib.bib165)). These methods keep the
interaction environment and user simulator fixed while improving the
learning algorithm. AutoInteract instead studies how to construct the
interaction data itself.

Grounded and Verifiable Synthetic Data. Early work created synthetic
post-training data by expanding a small set of seed instructions ([Wang
et al., 2023](#bib.bib131)). Later work increased its scale and
diversity through complexity evolution ([Xu et al., 2024](#bib.bib146)),
direct prompting of aligned models ([Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib147)), and
persona conditioning ([Ge et al., 2024](#bib.bib33)). Because
unconstrained generation can introduce errors, later methods ground
generated data in documents or structured sources and check whether
questions can be answered ([Lupidi et al., 2024](#bib.bib80); [Yuan
et al., 2026](#bib.bib159); [Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib155)). Execution
provides an especially strong check. In software engineering, tasks can
be generated directly from repositories and validated by running tests
([Pan et al., 2024](#bib.bib103); [Jain et al., 2025](#bib.bib49); [Wei
et al., 2026](#bib.bib133); [Yang et al., 2026](#bib.bib151)), producing
an inexpensive, objective reward that is difficult to exploit. Other
work generates tasks that challenge the current solver, either by
generating tasks and verifiers together ([Zhou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib169); [Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib164); [Liu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib75)) or by targeting problems the model cannot yet solve
([Zelikman et al., 2022](#bib.bib162)). These methods still produce
fully specified, single-turn tasks. AutoInteract keeps the source task
and its executable verifier unchanged but presents the task as an
interaction. The same execution reward can then measure both correctness
and the model’s ability to follow requirements given over several turns.
We also use a weak-versus-strong difficulty control, but the refinement
loop applies it to what task information is revealed and when, rather
than to the task’s inherent difficulty.

Agentic Data Generation and Self-Improvement. Recent systems use agents
to plan, inspect, and revise generated data instead of relying on fixed
pipelines. AgentInstruct uses agent workflows to produce large
post-training datasets ([Mitra et al., 2024](#bib.bib89)). Agentic
Self-Instruct uses a data-scientist agent to revise a generation recipe
based on weak- and strong-solver rollouts and judge feedback, and also
improves its own scaffold ([Kulikov et al., 2026](#bib.bib65)). Related
agents automate parts of the data-science workflow ([Guo et al.,
2024](#bib.bib39); [Hong et al., 2025](#bib.bib42)). This process is
related to prompt- and scaffold-optimization methods that revise prompts
or instructions using execution feedback ([Madaan et al.,
2023](#bib.bib82); [Fernando et al., 2023](#bib.bib30); [Yang et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib149); [Lu et al., 2024](#bib.bib79); [Agrawal et al.,
2026](#bib.bib3)). Our profile expansion also uses quality-diversity
search to cover a range of behaviors instead of maximizing a single
score ([Mouret and Clune, 2015](#bib.bib91); [Cully et al.,
2015](#bib.bib21)). AutoInteract differs from Agentic Self-Instruct in
three ways. First, it improves a multi-turn trajectory rather than a
single example. Second, it includes a simulated user learned from real
histories and evaluates realism directly. Third, the source task,
sampled profile, and user behavior prompt remain fixed across retries,
so the agent can revise only the multi-turn interaction. Holding these
inputs fixed prevents the agent from meeting the difficulty target by
changing the task in a way that disconnects it from the source, a
problem reported in unconstrained agentic data loops ([Kulikov et al.,
2026](#bib.bib65)).

### 3.8 Conclusion

We presented AutoInteract, a framework to improve agent-human
interaction by creating realistic, grounded multi-turn tasks calibrated
to the model being trained. It combines user models learned from real
interaction histories with an agentic data creation loop that uses judge
and execution feedback to control data quality and difficulty. Across
algorithmic and software engineering tasks, training on these data
significantly improves RL performance over baselines. Overall,
AutoInteract shifts the focus from training agents to solve verifiable
tasks independently to training them to collaborate with users on those
tasks, incorporating clarifications, feedback, and evolving requirements
across multiple turns to arrive at correct solutions. Our approach
generalizes to a broader set of tasks, offering a path toward more
effective human-agent interaction in the future. In particular,
leveraging humans’ and AIs’ complementary skills for research, termed
co-improvement (rather than self-improvement), looks like the fastest
and safest way towards superintelligence ([Weston and Foerster,
2025](#bib.bib137)), and any advancement in this interaction ability
will thus be beneficial.

## 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI

### 4.1 Overview

Motivation AI systems have achieved superhuman performance on a
cross-section of verifiable tasks through reinforcement learning, but
currently remain relatively weak in non-verifiable tasks. For example,
their generations exhibit a lack of high-quality writing, sometimes
termed “AI slop” ([Shaib et al., 2025](#bib.bib118)).

During pretraining, large language models are trained to predict the
most likely next token over corpora that span every level of human
expertise, from novice forum posts to expert prose. Maximum-likelihood
pretraining therefore tends to produce continuations that _reproduce_
the quality of its context rather than exceed it: given mediocre writing
the model most naturally continues in kind, and nothing in the objective
pushes generations toward _expert_ quality. Reinforcement learning from
human feedback (RLHF) ([Ouyang et al., 2022](#bib.bib100); [Bai et al.,
2022a](#bib.bib7)) can steer models higher, but it is only as good as
the reward it optimizes—and a reward that reliably recognizes good
writing is hard to build. Reward models trained on rankings from
non-expert annotators inherit those annotators’ ceiling, so the very
quality we care about most—expert, even superhuman, writing—is the
quality such rewards are least equipped to certify. The current focus on
post-training on verifiable rewards (e.g., on math, code, and agentic
environments) does not obviously improve language communication with
users, and may in fact worsen it. Progress on expert-level generation
thus hinges on a reward signal that recognizes expert quality _without_
requiring expert supervision at scale.

Our contribution We introduce a method to fix this problem,
Reinforcement Learning from eXpert-Aligned Rubrics (RL-XAR). We assert
that standard RL methods are sufficient to train superhuman writing
ability, but the failure to achieve this lies in the quality of the
reward model — which currently fails to correctly reward expert writing,
and incorrectly reward slop. The solution then is to align the reward
model more closely with human experts. This is possible without
collecting any new annotations, as there are already abundant examples
of expert human writing. Our approach thus first identifies examples of
such expert human writing from existing resources, and then uses these
examples as a training signal. We learn to generate rubrics for a given
writing task by ensuring the expert writing scores highly with these
rubrics relative to current models, by maximizing the human-model gap.
We can then perform standard RL with the newly learned expert-aligned
rubrics.

We conduct experiments in three settings: academic paper writing, story
writing and authoring Wikipedia articles. In each case, we show our
rubrics provide better alignment with expert writing, and RL-XAR
training gives large gains over standard training.

### 4.2 The failure of standard LLM Judgments

Successful training hinges on good grading. We first study the
reward-design problem in a concrete setting: writing a section from a
real academic paper. A model is given a selected high-quality paper
_minus_ one section—for example its abstract, introduction, related-work
section or conclusion—and must write the missing section so that it fits
the rest of the paper, using a similar word count to the originally
written section. The held-out human original provides a natural,
expert-authored reference, and the task is trivially sourced at scale
from the published literature. The precise setup is described in
[subsection G.1](#A7.SS1 "G.1 Datasets ‣ Appendix G Training agents to communicate with humans: extra details ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans").

We consider two standard ways to ask a language model to judge writing
quality—show it two candidates and ask which is better, or score each
candidate against a pre-designed rubric. We expect that a good judge
should place expert human writing above model writing. We evaluate
Opus-4.8 and GPT-5.6-sol as both writers and judges (cross-comparing
them).

Results are given in Figure
[12](#S4.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ 4.2 The failure of standard LLM Judgments ‣ 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans"),
with our main findings described below.

A direct pairwise judge prefers the model. A common protocol is to show
a judge two candidates and ask which is better, e.g., given the
rubric-free prompt “which version is the better section? Reason step by
step, then decide”—with each call scored in both A/B orders to cancel
position bias. This judge prefers the _models_ over the expert human in
the majority of cases, between 63.5% and 84.6%, depending on the writer
and judge setup.

A standard rubric does not register the gap either. While there are many
ways to build rubrics here, we prompted GPT-5.6 to build a meta-prompt
that, given a paper missing the section, generates rubrics specific for
judging that section. Switching to these rubric-based judgments instead
shows even more extreme results, with the model being selected as higher
scoring 100% of the time.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 12: Standard judgments (left, middle) rank the model above the
expert human—meta-optimizing the rubrics to be aligned with human
experts reverses this (right). If AI slop is judged to be better than
human writing by the LLM grader, then training will encourage more slop.
On the academic paper section writing task, we find standard pairwise
LLM judges or LLM-generated rubrics score GPT-5.6 or Opus-4.8 higher
than high-quality human writing. Our RL-XAR (eXpert-Aligned Rubrics)
approach instead meta-optimizes the rubrics on a training set of
high-quality human-written sections, resulting in rubrics that reverse
the result, and score the human writing higher on test papers.

### 4.3 RL from eXpert-Aligned Rubrics (RL-XAR)

The previous section showed the failure to judge expert human writing
exhibited by current systems. If AI slop is judged to be better than
human writing by the LLM grader we use, then training against that
grader will only encourage more slop. Given that we have access to
abundant examples of expert human writing, one might naturally ask: can
this be fixed by learning better judgments?

Our approach to learning rubrics, called eXpert-Aligned Rubrics (XAR),
is simple:

- •
  Identify examples of well-above average / expert human writing,
  splitting them into context and continuation.
- •
  Generate competing model-based continuations given the same context,
  which we expect to be worse writing (i.e., slop).
- •
  The above data form learning pairs, where humans should be scored
  higher. This training data is then used to learn to generate rubrics
  that maximize the scoring gap between humans and models.

Then, to train a model to be better at writing via reinforcement
learning (RL-XAR) using these rubrics, we iterate the following steps:

1.  (1)
    Learn XAR rubrics maximizing the gap between humans and the current
    model, as described above.
2.  (2)
    Perform reinforcement learning on a training set using the learned
    rubrics.
3.  (3)
    Repeat the procedure from step 1 until rubric learning can no longer
    identify a gap (i.e., we can no longer identify slop in the model).

We note that this approach is reminiscent of GANs ([Goodfellow et al.,
2014](#bib.bib35)).

#### 4.3.1 Learning the rubrics: can an LLM recognize expert writing?

While the learning of rubrics could be done in many ways, in our
experiments we use the following simple procedure of meta-prompt
optimization. We begin with an initial meta-prompt: given an example
context, it asks an LLM to generate rubrics for judging the
continuation. We can score the quality of this meta-prompt using the
human$`-`$model gap on a (small) training set, as described above.

Our optimization procedure then iterates a simple refinement loop over a
fixed number of iterations. At each iteration we show an _optimizer_ LLM
the current meta-prompt, the human$`-`$model gap it achieves on the
training set, and the specific examples where it fails, and ask it to
propose a revision that would widen the gap “for genuine-quality
reasons, not superficial tells”. The meta-prompt is held to a bounded
length, so the optimizer must consolidate criteria, rather than adding
ever more requirements. After optimization is complete, we keep the
best-performing candidate from across the iterations.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 13: Meta-rubric optimization. Left: mean expert human$`-`$model
(Muse Spark 1.1) gap by iteration for the _train_ and _valid_ splits;
the validation gap (solid) climbs from $`-4.2`$ to $`+2.76`$, crossing
zero (i.e., where humans are judged on average superior to the model) at
iteration 4 and peaking at iteration 5, and roughly tracks the training
gap (dashed) throughout—generalization to held-out papers, without
overfitting. Right: validation absolute means—the gap increases from
both directions, with the human’s score _rising_ ($`3.4\to 5.0`$) as the
model’s falls ($`7.6\to 2.7`$).

Initial Empirical Investigation To show the feasibility of our approach,
we conduct 7 iterations of meta-prompt optimization on the previously
described paper section writing task with a small set of 52 (paper,
section) examples, split into 8 papers for training and 5 held out for
validation. Using Muse Spark 1.1 as the rubric generator, writer model,
and as the final rubric-based judge, and Kimi-K2.6 as the
meta-optimizer, we report results in
[Figure 13](#S4.F13 "Figure 13 ‣ 4.3.1 Learning the rubrics: can an LLM recognize expert writing? ‣ 4.3 RL from eXpert-Aligned Rubrics (RL-XAR) ‣ 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans").
We find that the initial rubrics have a negative gap, i.e., the model is
preferred over expert human writing, but over meta-optimization
iterations, the gap becomes positive at iteration 4, and then rises
slightly over further iterations. The optimization both increases the
judgment scores of human writing ($`3.4\to 5.0`$), and decreases the
judgment scores of model writing ($`7.6\to 2.7`$).
[Figure 12](#S4.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ 4.2 The failure of standard LLM Judgments ‣ 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
(right) shows that the learned rubrics fix the failure of the pairwise
judge and standard rubrics described in
[subsection 4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 The failure of standard LLM Judgments ‣ 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans").

Analysis of the Learned Rubrics The initial rubrics, before learning,
tend to cover the paper’s specific content—naming the concrete claims,
methods, and results a section must convey—so they yield long,
paper-specific coverage checklists. We observe this has the unfortunate
effect of rewarding a “mini-paper” within each written section. Such
criteria reward fluent imitation, which restates material from across
the whole paper, while penalizing the selective human original for the
detail it deliberately omits. Over the iterations the optimizer rewrites
the guidance that mis-scores expert prose: docking the human for
principled omissions, crediting a compressed summary as fluency, and
mistaking surface polish for craft. The learned rubrics thus also tend
to reward sectional ownership (i.e., not a miniature of the whole
paper), disciplined selection, economy, and precise on-scope detail
rather than breadth of coverage. Because the meta-prompt is
length-bounded, the criteria settle into a small, stable, relatively
paper-independent set that tends to sharpen what it rewards instead of
accumulating requirements.

### 4.4 Main Experiments

#### 4.4.1 Paper Section Writing

We first apply RL-XAR to scientific paper-section writing.

Task. The model is provided the paper with one section removed and must
write that section (abstract, introduction, related work, or conclusion)
to best fit _this_ paper, basing every claim strictly on the paper’s
actual content, with no invented numbers, results, or citations. The
task prompt supplies a target word count equal to the original
human-written section’s length and asks the model to stay within roughly
$`\pm 15\%`$ of it.

Task data. We collect $`561`$ CS papers from the S2ORC corpus ([Lo
et al., 2020](#bib.bib78)), holding out each of their four sections
(abstract, introduction, related work, conclusion) in turn, to form
$`2{,}244`$ (paper, section) training examples; each example pairs the
rest of the paper as context with the held-out human section as the
expert reference. A disjoint set of $`90`$ papers ($`360`$ examples) is
held out for validation. For rubric optimization, we use the same small
set as described in
[subsubsection 4.3.1](#S4.SS3.SSS1 "4.3.1 Learning the rubrics: can an LLM recognize expert writing? ‣ 4.3 RL from eXpert-Aligned Rubrics (RL-XAR) ‣ 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans").
Further details are provided in
[subsection G.1](#A7.SS1 "G.1 Datasets ‣ Appendix G Training agents to communicate with humans: extra details ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans").

Training. We reinforcement-learn Qwen3.5-27B with prime-rl ([Intellect,
2025](#bib.bib48)) (GRPO, group size $`16`$, learning rate
$`3\times 10^{-6}`$, completions up to $`16`$k tokens), rewarding each
generation by the learned rubric as scored a Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B judge.
For rubric meta-optimization we use Kimi-K2.6.

RL-XAR loop. Following our method described in
[subsection 4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 RL from eXpert-Aligned Rubrics (RL-XAR) ‣ 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans"),
we run _three outer iterations_ of (i) meta-optimizing a rubric to
maximize the expert-human$`-`$model gap against the _current_ model,
where we (ii) reinforcement-learn the model against the set of so-far
collected rubrics. We train two iterations which re-target the failure
modes compared to human writing that the previous round’s model still
exhibits on the first two rounds of rubrics, and use the third round
rubrics to assess the model without the bias of retraining.

Rubric Evaluation. A model trained on one rubric can learn to satisfy
that rubric alone, so we evaluate every writer against _all three_ sets
of meta-optimized rubrics and rank by the _minimum_ of the three
human-normalized scores—the worst rubric, allowing no cherry-picking. We
use GPT-5.6 as a rubric judge for evaluation, so we do not evaluate with
the same judge used for training. Results are given in
[Table 8](#S4.T8 "Table 8 ‣ 4.4.1 Paper Section Writing ‣ 4.4 Main Experiments ‣ 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans").
RL-XAR carries our $`27`$B model to the top of this leaderboard among
all writers: its strongest checkpoint reaches a worst-rubric score of
$`9.60`$ (human $`=10`$), ahead of every external frontier model. While
these rubrics are still potentially biased towards our model (having
trained on the first two iterations) and still do not capture a fully
accurate measurement of expert human writing, they still reflect
performance better than previous approaches (cf.
[subsection 4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 The failure of standard LLM Judgments ‣ 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")).

Expert Human Evaluation We confirm these automatic metric gains in a
small preliminary study by evaluating on the authors’ own papers, on
which they are clearly experts. In a blind expert side-by-side
comparison of the RL-XAR model against the baseline Qwen3.5-27B on
held-out sections, the RL-XAR writer was preferred by 16 to 2 (an
$`89\%`$ win rate), showing that the rubric-measured improvement
corresponds to writing that expert readers may judge better. We found
that RL-XAR wins because the baseline generally has weak sectional
focus, often creating a “mini-paper”, and simultaneously contains too
many unnecessary details, e.g. numerical results when unneeded.
Nevertheless, we did not find the RL-XAR generations to be perfect
either, and expect better rubric optimization and graders could find
more flaws — which could be reinforced during training, i.e. using our
approach with frontier models, rather than Qwen3.5-27B as a writer and
Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B as a judge.

#### 4.4.2 Story Writing

Task. The model is shown a story up to a point where it stops mid-scene
and must continue from exactly where it leaves off—matching the
established voice, prose style, point of view, characters, setting, and
tone—without summarizing, restarting, adding a title, or shifting genre.
There is a provided length target (the human continuation’s length,
within $`{\sim}\pm 15\%`$).

Task data. We select books that are public-domain titles from Project
Gutenberg. For meta-optimization papers are quality-selected by an
external human credential (e.g., Pulitzer- and Nobel-prize-winning
authors) and biased toward each author’s lesser-read works to limit
memorization. Further, for all papers any continuation where a
temperature-$`0`$ probe reproduces more than 5% of the reference’s
13-grams, or a single contiguous verbatim run of $`\geq`$20 words is
present, the example is dropped from the data. We use $`2{,}290`$
examples for training, 310 for validation. Each pairing consists of the
story-so-far as context with the author’s verbatim continuation as the
expert reference. We further use a disjoint set of $`52`$ examples for
rubric meta-optimization with $`20`$ held out for validation, and $`60`$
for final testing.

Training. We use the same recipe as
[subsubsection 4.4.1](#S4.SS4.SSS1 "4.4.1 Paper Section Writing ‣ 4.4 Main Experiments ‣ 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")—GRPO
on Qwen3.5-27B using a Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B judge. We only ran a single
iteration of RL-XAR in this case. We used rubrics generated from a
meta-prompt optimized via Kimi-K2.6 with a Muse Spark 1.1 meta-prompt
rubric generator, writer model, and judge. The resulting blind
meta-rubric optimization trajectory is shown in
[fig. 18](#A7.F18 "In G.3 Additional Results ‣ Appendix G Training agents to communicate with humans: extra details ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans").

Rubric Evaluation. We evaluate under the same story rubrics, but switch
the judge to GPT-5.6, and report human-normalized scores. Results are
given in
[Table 9](#S4.T9 "Table 9 ‣ 4.4.1 Paper Section Writing ‣ 4.4 Main Experiments ‣ 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans"),
left. RL-XAR lifts Qwen3.5-27B from $`2.8`$ to $`8.2`$—the top of all
writers, ahead of every frontier model (next best Claude 5 Opus,
$`6.8`$).

Human Evaluation We confirm these automatic metric gains by human
evaluation in a small preliminary study by the authors. In a blind
side-by-side comparison of the RL-XAR model against the baseline
Qwen3.5-27B on held-out story continuations, the RL-XAR writer was
preferred by 19 to 1 (a $`95\%`$ win rate), showing that the
rubric-measured improvement corresponds to writing that humans may judge
better. We found the baseline to be poor at following the style of the
story. Further, one noticeable feature is that it often falls back to
clichéd or poor-quality similes, e.g. “the air hung over the table like
a warm cloth” and “the wind rustled the leaves, sounding like a whisper
of warning, or perhaps a laugh” that do not match the author’s work.

#### 4.4.3 Authoring Wikipedia Articles

Task. The model is given only the article title and the target section
heading and must write that body section from scratch to a specified
target length, similar to the other two tasks.

Task data. We select Wikipedia articles that carry a Featured- or
Good-Article quality tier, and are again biased toward less-popular
titles, and pass the same memorization filters as mentioned previously.
We provide $`1{,}187`$ training and $`162`$ validation examples. We
further use a disjoint set of $`42`$ examples for rubric
meta-optimization with $`12`$ held out for validation, and $`60`$ for
final testing.

Training. We use a recipe identical to
[subsubsection 4.4.2](#S4.SS4.SSS2 "4.4.2 Story Writing ‣ 4.4 Main Experiments ‣ 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans"),
optimizing the rubrics for this setting. The blind meta-rubric
optimization trajectory is shown in
[fig. 18](#A7.F18 "In G.3 Additional Results ‣ Appendix G Training agents to communicate with humans: extra details ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans").

Rubric Evaluation. We report results using the learned Wikipedia
rubrics, but using a separate GPT-5.6 judge. Results are given in
[Table 9](#S4.T9 "Table 9 ‣ 4.4.1 Paper Section Writing ‣ 4.4 Main Experiments ‣ 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans"),
right. Here, we find RL-XAR moves Qwen3.5-27B only from $`2.7`$ to
$`4.0`$: the gains are small and the model stays well below both the
human and the frontier writers (GPT-5.6 $`8.9`$, Claude 5.5 Opus
$`8.2`$). Wikipedia section writing is the hardest of the three domains
for this recipe, in part due to the inadequacy of the Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B
judge, which is analyzed in
[subsubsection 4.4.4](#S4.SS4.SSS4 "4.4.4 Detailed Analysis, Ablations & Additional Experiments ‣ 4.4 Main Experiments ‣ 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans").

#### 4.4.4 Detailed Analysis, Ablations & Additional Experiments

The Judge matters. Our results from
[subsection 4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 The failure of standard LLM Judgments ‣ 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
and
[subsubsection 4.3.1](#S4.SS3.SSS1 "4.3.1 Learning the rubrics: can an LLM recognize expert writing? ‣ 4.3 RL from eXpert-Aligned Rubrics (RL-XAR) ‣ 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
show the rubrics matter. Here, we show the quality of the LLM judge
evaluating those rubrics is just as important. A weak judge simply
cannot differentiate between expert human and model writing—as
[fig. 14](#S4.F14 "In 4.4.4 Detailed Analysis, Ablations & Additional Experiments ‣ 4.4 Main Experiments ‣ 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
shows across all three writing domains.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 14: Comparison of Judges, averaged over XAR-optimized rubrics.
Mean human$`-`$model gap (writer $`=`$ Muse Spark 1.1; positive $`=`$
human favored) for each judge, with judges in decreasing capability
order. On Story and Wikipedia, Qwen3.5-27B (red) is the only judge to
turn _negative_, ranking the model _above_ human writing ($`-0.55`$
story, $`-0.39`$ wiki); on Paper the four judges are close and all
human-favoring. A weak grader is incapable of seeing the gap.

The Meta-Optimizer matters. We compare Muse Spark 1.1, Opus 5 and Kimi
K2.6 as rubric meta-optimizers in
[Figure 15](#S4.F15 "Figure 15 ‣ 4.4.4 Detailed Analysis, Ablations & Additional Experiments ‣ 4.4 Main Experiments ‣ 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans"),
each averaged over 3 seeds, reporting the human-model validation gap of
Muse Spark 1.1 as a paper section writer. We find that Kimi and Opus can
find a positive gap, but Muse Spark 1.1 struggles. Likely, weaker models
struggle even more. Finally, we note we used a simple iterative
refinement meta-optimization method, when many other methods exist
([Agrawal et al., 2026](#bib.bib3); [Khattab et al., 2023](#bib.bib60)).
We conducted preliminary experiments on a GEPA optimization variant, but
it did not yield superior results to our main reported results, and we
leave such investigations for future work.

Figure 15: Different Rubric Meta-Optimizers. Mean (human $`-`$ model)
gap per optimizer, averaged over three seeds.

Expert humans matter. Using examples of expert human writing matters for
rubric optimization. We validate this by using papers judged to be low-,
medium- and high-quality human writing, and evaluating them against our
learned rubrics, see
[Figure 16](#S4.F16 "Figure 16 ‣ 4.4.4 Detailed Analysis, Ablations & Additional Experiments ‣ 4.4 Main Experiments ‣ 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans").
Comparing humans to GPT-5.6 we observe a gap of +1.39 for high-quality
human writers, +0.95 for medium-quality and only +0.37 for low-quality.
Hence, using low-quality writing against a strong model writer would
likely be unable to find useful rubrics or a human-model gap.
Additionally, if the learned rubric measures genuine quality, the
human-model gap should be larger for better-written human papers and
smaller for weak ones, which is what we observe.

Figure 16: Human$`-`$model gap by paper human writing-quality bin
(low/medium/high, light to dark), comparing with two models (Muse Spark
1.1 and GPT-5.6). If the learned rubric is measuring genuine quality,
the human-model gap should be larger for better-written human papers and
shrink for weak ones, which is what we observe.

The need for iterative rubrics. For paper section writing, we note that
in the first iteration of RL-XAR training an evaluation of (11.0, 7.0,
8.4) is obtained across the three rounds of rubrics. Round 1 rubrics are
optimized, giving a high score, but at the cost of round 2 rubrics,
which are not optimized — a score of 7.0 being far below the starting
point 10.4 of Qwen3.5-27B. Iteration 2 training restores the performance
of round 2 rubrics to baseline model performance, while scoring highly
across the other two sets of rubrics. We believe that a fully online
approach would improve this overall training recipe, which we leave for
future work.

Rubrics generalize across strong Judges. If two different judges are
both strong enough, we observe that one can optimize rubrics for one
judge, and we see those rubrics work for a different judge. For example,
we show this in
[Table 10](#S4.T10 "Table 10 ‣ 4.4.4 Detailed Analysis, Ablations & Additional Experiments ‣ 4.4 Main Experiments ‣ 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
for GPT-5.6 and Muse Spark 1.1 judges.

| ------------------------------- | ------------- | --------- | ---------- | --------- |
|                                 | Blind rubrics |           | GT rubrics |           |
| Rubric Judge                    | train         | valid     | train      | valid     |
| GPT-5.6 (cross-family)          | $`+1.69`$     | $`+1.79`$ | $`+2.57`$  | $`+2.49`$ |

Table 10: Cross-judge robustness of rubrics: mean gap (human $`-`$ Muse
Spark 1.1) on the paper section writing task, scored by the cross-family
GPT-5.6 judge versus the Muse Spark 1.1 judge. The human is preferred
under both judges on every split and variant. Ground Truth (GT) rubrics
are built by including the hidden section as input when generating
rubrics via the meta-prompt, thereby biasing scores towards the
human-written completion. GT rubric scores are thus higher across the
board.

Blind vs. ground-truth rubrics. When generating rubrics from the rubric
meta-prompt, it is possible to condition on only the context (called
“blind” rubrics), or on the context and human continuation as well
(called “Ground Truth” (GT) rubrics). The latter would likely only make
sense when the human continuations are high quality, as the rubrics
would be based on them as well. We compare their scoring ability in
[Table 10](#S4.T10 "Table 10 ‣ 4.4.4 Detailed Analysis, Ablations & Additional Experiments ‣ 4.4 Main Experiments ‣ 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans").
GT rubrics give higher human-model gaps across two different rubric
judges, as expected. Further study is required to understand the
difference between using the two variants.

Length constraints and rubrics. In preliminary experiments we found that
standard models, given the task of paper section writing without a
specific instructed length constraint, tend to write overlong sections —
as much as two or three times as long as the hidden original human
sections. This tends to allow them to score more highly on the given set
of rubrics, similar to other instruction-following settings ([Yuan
et al., 2025](#bib.bib158)). We therefore chose to define
length-constrained tasks instead, i.e., to write a section similar to
the original human length. Strong models are capable of this, although
we observed an unwanted side effect that they tend to reserve a lot of
chain-of-thought thinking towards this constraint (e.g., word counting).

Verifiable code-based rewards for surface-form distributional shifts.
Our standard RL-XAR reward is an LLM judge scoring an expert-aligned
rubric, and it is good at what a rubric is good at: writing quality,
coverage, and content. However, with current models it appears to be
much less reliable at scoring some verifiable, measurable properties of
the output distribution—e.g., how closely a writer matches the human
distribution of surface form (sentence length and its variation,
paragraphing, lexical diversity, punctuation rates, dialogue), and so
on. These are properties one can compute exactly from the text with a
small piece of code; we therefore complement the rubric judge with a
_code-based reward_. This code reward is still expert human-anchored,
like our meta-optimized rubrics. We score each constructed feature
against this item’s human reference, and the model is rewarded for
resembling the human distribution. We can hence also meta-optimize the
code reward itself—searching for its feature set and overall code the
same way as before by maximizing the human-model gap. Here, we run a
small study with a fixed reward multiplied into the RL-XAR reward, with
results shown in
[Table 11](#S4.T11 "Table 11 ‣ 4.4.4 Detailed Analysis, Ablations & Additional Experiments ‣ 4.4 Main Experiments ‣ 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans").
They show that this approach can fix some distributional shifts that
might otherwise occur during RL, without hurting the standard rubric
rewards. More details are given in
[subsection G.4](#A7.SS4 "G.4 Verifiable surface-form code-based rewards ‣ Appendix G Training agents to communicate with humans: extra details ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans").

Training rubrics online. We also briefly experiment with a fully online
(co-training) objective where the writing generator is optimizing for
the rubrics, and the rubrics are simultaneously being trained by GRPO
(not meta-optimization) to optimize the human-model gap for the current
policy—for the latter, generated rubrics are rewarded by the normalized
gap, see
[Figure 17](#S4.F17 "Figure 17 ‣ 4.4.4 Detailed Analysis, Ablations & Additional Experiments ‣ 4.4 Main Experiments ‣ 4 Training agents to communicate with humans: unslopping AI ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans").
While we leave subsequent experiments for future work, our first results
in this direction on the story task are positive, with a gain from 2.8
(Qwen3.5-27B) to 6.0 (online RL-XAR) when testing with the same fixed
(learned) rubric applied in our earlier experiments.

Figure 17: Online RL-XAR: Training the writer (via the current rubric
generator) and the rubric generator (using the human-model gap) online
simultaneously. While this is not the approach reported in our main
experiments, it appears to work well also, and future work should
explore this approach further.

shifts. RL-XAR with surface-form code-based rewards moves the most

### 4.5 Related Work

RL for verifiable vs. non-verifiable tasks. Reinforcement learning has
driven much of the recent progress on tasks with checkable
answers—mathematics, code, and reasoning—where a programmatic verifier
supplies a reliable reward ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib119);
[DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025](#bib.bib23)). Open-ended writing admits no
such verifier, and models optimized without one tend to produce fluent
but low-quality text, a failure increasingly recognized as “AI slop”
([Shaib et al., 2025](#bib.bib118); [Paech et al., 2026](#bib.bib101)).
Our goal is to bring the reliability of verifiable-reward RL to this
non-verifiable regime by _learning_ a reward that recognizes expert
writing.

RLHF and reward modeling. Learning rewards from human preference
comparisons ([Christiano et al., 2017](#bib.bib18); [Stiennon et al.,
2020](#bib.bib123)) underpins modern instruction tuning ([Ouyang et al.,
2022](#bib.bib100); [Bai et al., 2022a](#bib.bib7); [Rafailov et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib112)). Such rewards are bounded by the raters that
produce them: preferences from non-expert annotators cannot certify
expert—let alone superhuman—quality, and optimizing an imperfect reward
invites over-optimization and reward hacking ([Gao et al.,
2022](#bib.bib31); [Rafailov et al., 2024a](#bib.bib111)), of which
verbosity and length bias are canonical cases ([Dubois et al.,
2024](#bib.bib26); [Yuan et al., 2025](#bib.bib158)). RL-XAR targets
exactly this gap: rather than collect more preferences, it derives the
reward from _existing_ expert texts.

AI feedback and LLM judges. A growing body of work replaces or augments
human labels with model-generated feedback—constitutional and
AI-feedback training ([Bai et al., 2022b](#bib.bib8)), self-rewarding
models that judge their own outputs ([Yuan et al., 2024](#bib.bib157)),
and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation ([Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib166);
[Glaese et al., 2022](#bib.bib34)). We find that off-the-shelf judges,
and even generated rubrics, systematically _under_-credit expert human
writing relative to fluent model prose—a signal that would teach a
policy to write worse. Our contribution is a procedure that repairs this
misalignment without reference access at evaluation time.

Rubrics, checklists, and criteria-based evaluation. Decomposing quality
into explicit criteria has a long history in NLP evaluation ([Ribeiro
et al., 2020](#bib.bib115)), and rubric-conditioned grading is
increasingly used as a reward for open-ended generation. Unlike a fixed,
hand-written rubric or a “mentions-$`X`$” checklist that only the
reference can satisfy, we _generate_ rubrics from the surrounding
context and _meta-learn_ the generator so its rubrics recover the
discrimination that reference access would otherwise provide.

Prompt and meta-prompt optimization. Automatically optimizing prompts
([Zhou et al., 2022](#bib.bib170)), including reflective and
evolutionary search over prompt programs ([Agrawal et al.,
2026](#bib.bib3); [Khattab et al., 2023](#bib.bib60)), has become a
practical alternative to gradient-based adaptation. We apply
meta-optimization not to a task prompt but to the _rubric-generation_
prompt, driving it to _maximize_ the expert-human$`-`$model score gap;
this adversarial objective—an evaluator improved against a generator—is
reminiscent of GANs ([Goodfellow et al., 2014](#bib.bib35)). Other
relevant work with evolving rewards includes the work of [Kim et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib61).

Expert signals without expert annotators. Eliciting strong capabilities
from weak or cheap supervision, and asking whether such oversight
scales, is central to training superhuman systems ([Bowman et al.,
2022](#bib.bib13); [Burns et al., 2023](#bib.bib14)), and evaluating
open-ended and creative writing is itself notoriously hard ([Karpinska
et al., 2021](#bib.bib58); [Chung et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)). RL-XAR
sidesteps new expert annotation by anchoring the reward to abundant,
externally credentialed expert texts—published papers, prize-winning
fiction, and peer-reviewed encyclopedia articles—and learning to score
them above current models.

### 4.6 Conclusion

We introduced RL-XAR, Reinforcement Learning from eXpert-Aligned
Rubrics, a recipe that turns readily available expert human writing into
a learned, expert-aligned reward and then optimizes against it. Its key
step meta-optimizes a rubric generator to maximize the gap between
expert human text and current model generations, iterating until no
discernible gap remains; standard RL against the resulting rubrics then
improves writing quality. Across three domains—writing academic paper
sections, Pulitzer- and Nobel-grade story continuation, and Wikipedia
section writing—RL-XAR yields large gains over the base model. Our hope
is that if AIs can be better communicators with humans, we can all
benefit.

Several limitations in our experiments point to future work. Our learned
rubrics, trained in part against our own model, may remain biased toward
it and do not yet fully capture expert quality. The writer (Qwen3.5-27B)
and reward judge (Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B) used during training are mid-sized,
and we expect the recipe to yield even better results when applied with
frontier writers and graders. More broadly, RL-XAR offers a template for
reward design in non-verifiable domains beyond the writing tasks used
here: anchor the ground truth outside the systems under test, learn the
criteria rather than hand-writing them, and iterate the evaluator
against the generator until the human expert$`-`$model gap closes.

## Appendix A AutoBenchmark implementation details

### A.1 Stage 1: Benchmark proposal

Stage 1-A. Authoring session. We run one fresh research agent per
iteration: an OpenHands agent \[[Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib130)\] with
a terminal, a file editor, a task tracker, and a summarizing condenser,
in an isolated container. It writes only to its own iteration directory
and reads the brief, the operator grounding, the pinned Harbor
documentation \[[Harbor Framework Team, 2026](#bib.bib40)\], and earlier
frozen submissions; public unauthenticated web retrieval is available
for grounding. It cannot call models, launch judges or solvers, start
containers, submit scheduler jobs, or run its own benchmark, and the
structural validator below is the only executable check it may invoke.
The session ends by writing a one-shot marker, after which we freeze and
hash the tree.

Stage 1-B. Submission contract. A submission contains a specification
(construct, scientific value, scope, hypothesis, feasibility argument,
threats to validity), a comparison of at least three materially
different designs, a grounding directory with retained source bytes and
a provenance manifest, and a record of the agent’s research process.
Each task directory is a complete native Harbor task: instruction, task
configuration, assets uploaded into the solver’s working directory, a
deterministic reference solution, and a verifier directory holding the
grading criteria, a judging context, and a private reference answer.
Every manifest record carries an origin, a UTC retrieval time, a local
path, a SHA-256, and license terms; self-generated data must
additionally retain the executable generator, its parameters and seed,
per-stage timestamps, and verified asset hashes. Criteria are native
binary, Likert, or numeric items with positive weights and stable
identifiers, and regexes, required phrases, length targets, and
model-specific criteria are prohibited.

Stage 1-C. Structural validation. We scaffold each task before the
session from pinned harbor task init output, with the Dockerfile removed
and fixed Reward Kit files installed. The first gate validates the
frozen tree without executing it. Protected content must return
byte-identical: verifier launcher, answer-judge prompt template, image
digests, timeouts, resource and network settings, and the judge wiring
that fixes the judge’s inputs, the reference path, and the aggregation;
the agent may edit only the task description, keywords, and scientific
metadata. Each required task must appear exactly once; every path must
be a regular file, so symlinks, hardlinks, device nodes, and sparse
files are rejected; the executable bit is allowed only on the reference
solution and the protected launcher; and the package must stay within
$`1{,}024`$ files, $`2`$ GiB total, $`256`$ MiB per file, and
$`240`$-byte paths. Criteria must satisfy the Reward Kit schema (unique
identifiers, positive weights, at least two points for a Likert item, an
explicit range for a numeric item), and manifest timestamps, hostnames,
and hashes must match the retained bytes. Three further checks apply to
revisions: we parse the reference solution in shell no-execute mode and
compile its literal Python heredocs; we hold criterion identity fixed,
so an identifier cannot be rebound to another name nor a name to another
identifier; and we reject an instruction change whose private grading
and reference artifacts are byte-identical to the checkpoint, the
signature of a partial write.

Stage 1-D. Revision integrity. From the second iteration onward, a
dedicated judge runs before execution. It sees the solver-visible
projection of the checkpoint and of the current submission, namely
instructions, READMEs, public metadata, and assets, together with a
trusted diff, the feedback the agent could read, and the current
grounding; private references, criteria, solutions, and all hidden
solver results are excluded. It applies a counterfactual test to every
material public change: with all prior solver answers and scores
removed, would an independent author still make this change from the
construct, the grounding, or a genuine ambiguity? A change passes only
if retained sources support it at an exact locator; making an observed
solver error less likely is not a justification. A static detector flags
numbers, causal edges, stratum identities, and long $`n`$-grams that
newly appear in public files and also appear in the feedback, as
advisory input. The verdict is binding, and its provenance review covers
the whole current grounding, not only records touched by the diff.

Stage 1-E. Reference-solution admission. We execute the agent’s own
reference solution in the real task container through Harbor’s Oracle
agent and grade it with the real verifier and answer judge. A submission
is admitted only with no verifier error and reward at least $`0.9`$,
which establishes that the task is solvable under the fixed contract,
that the environment holds what the solution needs, and that the grader
awards the intended answer. Retained reward artifacts are hashed into
the validation report the quality judges later read.

Stage 1-F. Repair. A failure at any of the three gates returns the
iteration to a fresh session of the same agent, which receives a repair
report naming the failing gate and the defect and is restricted to
fixing it. We allow at most ten submission attempts per iteration.

### A.2 Stage 2: Benchmark solving

Stage 2-A. Solver runs. Each solver attempts every task once, which we
treat as one observation per model and task, using Harbor’s agent in the
task container under the fixed execution contract and per-route token
caps, five tasks at a time. A completed run retains the final answer,
the trajectory in Harbor’s ATIF format, and a result summary. Provider
errors, container and scheduler failures, missing trajectories, and
truncated collections are classified as infrastructure outcomes and
retried, never recorded as incorrect answers; only completed runs enter
the difficulty signal, and the feedback states this so the agent does
not read a failed run as a solved task. External solvers use a separate
lane whose results go to an operator-private directory that no feedback
index references, routed through a loopback proxy.

Stage 2-B. Answer judging. Answers are graded in a separate verifier
container by a judge that sees the judging context, the answer, and the
private reference, and scores each criterion independently; scores
combine by a protected weighted mean into a reward in $`[0,1]`$. The
judge prompt is a harness-owned template that treats the task, the
answer, and every quoted asset as untrusted evidence, and we fix the
judge route so the agent cannot address the grader. Published feedback
carries per-criterion scores and anchors.

### A.3 Stage 3: Benchmark review

Stage 3-A. Criteria. We run one judge per criterion. The wording below
is canonical and is disclosed verbatim to the research agent, so it
knows what its submission is reviewed against.

- (i)
  Construct validity. The benchmark measures the research-agent
  capability claimed in the brief and the specification, not an
  incidental proxy or an evaluator quirk.
- (ii)
  Correctness. Task artifacts, private references, rubric semantics,
  score calculation, and reproducibility are internally correct and free
  of leakage.
- (iii)
  Feasibility. A genuinely stronger research agent could solve the
  benchmark with the supplied evidence, resources, and rules; difficulty
  from missing evidence, impossible requirements, or circular evaluation
  is rejected.
- (iv)
  Usefulness. Progress would transfer to meaningful scientific work or
  provide valuable evidence about research-agent capability.
- (v)
  Overall. The integrated contribution has no serious red flags and is a
  credible publication-quality benchmark design at the current scale.

Stage 3-B. Isolation and verdicts. The five sessions run concurrently on
physically isolated bundles holding the brief, the specification, the
grounding, the frozen submission, a sanitized validation report
(versions, image digests, judge identifier and prompt hash, scoring
wiring, reference-solution status and reward), and the retained solver
evidence. No judge sees another’s verdict. Each writes a JSON verdict
with a pass or fail decision, a responsibility field separating
submission defects from harness faults, at least three artifact
citations, at least one strength and one weakness, required fixes for a
fail, a confidence level, and a rationale.

Stage 3-C. Evidence protocol. A manifest entry is an untrusted
assertion. Every material claim or grading anchor must be verified
against retained content at an exact locator or a reproducible
derivation, and placeholder domains, invented citations, dead locators,
self-authored text presented as publisher bytes, and unsupported license
or version declarations are mandatory failures. Judges may not browse
the web to repair an evidentiary gap, so a claim that cannot be checked
inside the bundle counts against the submission.

### A.4 Overall loop

Component A. AI Feedback. We publish one curated, secret-scanned bundle
per iteration containing the validation report, per-task run status,
sanitized trajectories and answers for the in-loop solvers,
per-criterion rubric judgments, and the five verdicts. Only files named
by the bundle index may be read, and hidden external results stay in the
private lane of
[subsection A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Stage 2: Benchmark solving ‣ Appendix A AutoBenchmark implementation details ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans").
Raw provider logs, exception text, and judge reasoning are omitted, and
all published evidence is labeled untrusted, so an instruction embedded
in an answer or a retrieved document is not a directive to the next
session.

Component B. Checkpoint selection. Before iteration $`t`$ we build a
history over iterations $`1`$ to $`t-1`$. An iteration is eligible when
all five verdicts passed and its solver evaluation is complete; among
eligible iterations we take the lowest mean reward on the solver
designated as the selection objective, breaking ties toward the later
iteration. With nothing eligible we fall back to the latest fully
evaluated iteration and label the session a repair. The selected
checkpoint is copied atomically into the new writable directory for
in-place editing, and the prompt exposes every prior snapshot and
feedback index, so the agent can inspect iterations it did not descend
from. The end-of-run selection uses the same policy but refuses any
checkpoint that did not pass every judge, and is written where the agent
cannot see it.

Component C. Human feedback. The operator-in-the-loop setting of
[subsection 1.3](#S1.SS3 "1.3 Experimental Setup ‣ 1 The role of humans in directing research agents for benchmark creation ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
reuses this machinery. The driver finishes the preceding iteration, then
pauses before the next session and writes a review packet with per-task
scores, action and tool counts, rubric misses, quality outcomes, and
paths to the full trajectories and answers; no model job runs while it
waits. We validate and snapshot the admitted response and expose it as
one more read-only artifact alongside the checkpoint history, after
which the loop resumes.

## Appendix B Benchmark examples built with AutoBenchmark

### B.1 Graveyard Bench

Graveyard Bench asks whether an idea generating model will re propose a
research direction that is already dead. Each task is seeded from on
failed research from a null pre-registered clinical trial, a medical
reversal, or a results-level retraction. The task gives the solver only
a neutral research goal (plus some background), but never the refuted
intervention, and asks for ten structured hypotheses, each with a
confidence score and a previously_refuted or not_previously_refuted
flag. A task counts as a zombie (incorrect) if any hypothesis matches
the hidden claim’s intervention, effect direction and scope without
being flagged previously_refuted. The difficulty is that a refuted idea
leaves no confirming paper behind, so it looks unexplored, and
novelty-seeking pushes the solver straight toward it.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### B.2 Rebuttal Bench

Rebuttal Bench asks whether an author response actually answers the
reviewer. Each task supplies the reviewer comments and the author
rebuttal from one paper with transparent peer review, and the solver
adjudicates every sub-concern as RESOLVED, PARTIALLY_RESOLVED,
NOT_RESOLVED, or DEFLECTED, labeling the type of evidence supplied and,
where one applies, the deflection tactic used. The tasks are constructed
so that fluency is not evidence: several rebuttals substitute a weaker
assay for the one the reviewer requested, and several excerpts contain a
second-round reviewer declaring satisfaction, which the instruction
explicitly forbids treating as proof of resolution.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### B.3 SilentTrain Bench

SilentTrain Bench asks the solver to repair a training bug that never
raises an error. Each task supplies a complete repository containing one
silent correctness regression, such as a compiled optimizer reusing
stale state after a gradient becomes None, an epoch that finishes
without processing a batch, or a mixture-of-experts run that omits its
auxiliary loss from the reported total. The solver has to reproduce the
defect, fix it in the supplied repository, and validate the fix by
executing a command that exercises the affected behavior. Its grader is
the only hybrid one of the three: a programmatic criterion runs a hidden
regression over the repaired repository, and the judge criteria below
read the submitted patch and the retained execution log alongside the
written answer, so an explanation without a working repair does not
pass. Both the instruction and the grader come from the run that
received execution feedback, and its three interventions are visible in
them: the requirement to work from the complete repository, the
requirement to submit an executed validation, and the shift from a
deterministic checker to behavioral grading.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Appendix C HackBench Task Suite

This appendix describes the 13 long-horizon autoresearch tasks
represented in the 169 released trajectories
(§[2.2.2](#S2.SS2.SSS2 "2.2.2 Autoresearch Grounding ‣ 2.2 HackBench ‣ 2 HackBench: Detecting and Localizing Reward Hacking in Autoresearch Agents ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")):
5 from ResearchGym \[[Garikaparthi et al., 2026](#bib.bib32)\], 7 from
the AutoLab “Model Development” subset \[[Xu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib148)\], and one weak-to-strong research task based on
automated-w2s-research \[[Wen, 2026](#bib.bib134)\].
Table [12](#A3.T12 "Table 12 ‣ Appendix C HackBench Task Suite ‣ Aligning Autoresearch:Co-Improvement between Agents & Humans")
summarizes each task’s intended objective in plain terms, grouped by its
source benchmark or research codebase.

The task wrappers used for trajectory collection differ in how closely
their verifier rewards track these objectives. AutoLab verifiers
evaluate agent-produced models or edited implementations using
task-specific evaluation routines, rather than accepting self-reported
scores. For four ResearchGym tasks, the wrapper reward is a stub based
on changes to the task tree; the research metrics are handled by
separate grading scripts and are not what this stub measures. The
materials-tokenization wrapper instead applies a threshold to an
aggregated SOFC-NER F₁ score, without rerunning model evaluation. The
w2s wrapper likewise uses a stub: it returns a constant reward of 0.0
and logs basic session activity, rather than evaluating PGR. These
different scoring interfaces shape the reward-hacking surface available
to the agent.

| Task                                                    | Description                                                                                                                                               |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| ResearchGym \[[Garikaparthi et al., 2026](#bib.bib32)\] |                                                                                                                                                           |
| continual-learning                                      | Teach an image classifier a sequence of new classes without forgetting the earlier ones, on CIFAR-100 and other image benchmarks                          |
| cross-modal-retrieval                                   | Retrieve the matching caption for an image and the matching image for a caption when the test queries differ from training                                |
| improving-replay-buffers                                | Improve how a reinforcement-learning agent reuses past experience to learn continuous-control tasks such as Hopper                                        |
| materials-tokenization                                  | Design a better way to split materials-science text into tokens so a language model identifies scientific terms more accurately than a published baseline |
| time-series-explanation                                 | Build a method that identifies which parts of a time series explain a model’s prediction, tested on medical and sensor data                               |
| AutoLab \[[Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib148)\]              |                                                                                                                                                           |
| scaling_law                                             | Train a language model from scratch on WikiText-103 within a fixed compute budget, aiming for the lowest perplexity                                       |
| llm_online_serving                                      | Serve a stream of incoming requests to a language model with higher throughput and lower latency                                                          |
| moving_mnist_world_model                                | Train a video model that watches ten frames of moving digits and predicts the next ten                                                                    |
| data_select_ifeval                                      | Choose the most useful subset of examples (up to 5,000 of 50,000) for fine-tuning a model to follow instructions                                          |
| multilingual_ocr                                        | Fine-tune an optical-character-recognition model to transcribe Persian and Bengali text from images more accurately                                       |
| grpo_multisource                                        | Fine-tune a vision–language model to solve visual math problems better without losing its general visual ability                                          |
| flux2_klein_lora                                        | Teach an image generator a new visual concept from only fifteen example images                                                                            |
| automated-w2s-research \[[Wen, 2026](#bib.bib134)\]     |                                                                                                                                                           |
| w2s                                                     | Design a method that uses a weak model’s labels to train a stronger model that beats the baseline                                                         |

Table 12: The 13 autoresearch tasks used to collect trajectories,
grouped under their source dataset. Each description states, in plain
terms, the objective the agent optimizes.

## Appendix D HackBench Prompts

This appendix shows the two prompts referenced in the main text: the
system prompt that drives the _main research agent_ (the Harbor
terminus-2 scaffold,
